## TestimonyArguments.SolaScriptura.Results — what does and does not follow

The results this module exists for are the two on the hinge. The seed asserted
in prose that the dispute reduces to `solaScripturaIsTaughtByScripture`; here
that claim is split into the two roles the premise actually plays, because they
come apart.

#### The positions

<a id="protestant_establishes"></a>
**`protestant_establishes`**

Given the Protestant premises, on any of its three routes, the conclusion
follows.

```lean
theorem protestant_establishes : Establishes protestant
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="tradition0_establishes"></a>
**`tradition0_establishes`**

**Tradition 0 establishes it too.** Geisler rejects Mathison's claim that
tradition is hermeneutically necessary; he does not reject sola scriptura. The
position Mathison calls "solo scriptura" and judges unbiblical and unworkable
reaches the same conclusion by a different route, once it is stated by someone
who holds it rather than by its critic.

```lean
theorem tradition0_establishes : Establishes tradition0
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="tridentineReading"></a>
**`tridentineReading`**

The Tridentine reading, written down: tradition is a coordinate source, so
scripture is not the sole rule.

```lean
def tridentineReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.scriptureIsSoleInfallibleRule => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="tridentine_not_establishes"></a>
**`tridentine_not_establishes`**

The two-source premises do not establish sola scriptura — they entail its
negation.

```lean
theorem tridentine_not_establishes : ¬Establishes tridentine
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="magisterialReading"></a>
**`magisterialReading`**

The post-Vatican I reading: the magisterium is the living interpreter, so
scripture is not the sole infallible rule; and the apostles' office did not end
with them, but continues in the bishops.

```lean
def magisterialReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.apostlesOfficeEndedWithThem => False
    | Claim.scriptureIsSoleInfallibleRule => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="vaticanI_not_establishes"></a>
**`vaticanI_not_establishes`**

Tradition III likewise entails the negation — by a different premise from
Tradition II's, which is why the two are separate packages.

```lean
theorem vaticanI_not_establishes : ¬Establishes vaticanI
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="orthodoxReading"></a>
**`orthodoxReading`**

The Orthodox reading: the mind of the Church interprets infallibly, with no
magisterium and no second source of revelation.

```lean
def orthodoxReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.scriptureIsSoleInfallibleRule => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="orthodox_not_establishes"></a>
**`orthodox_not_establishes`**

Orthodoxy also entails the negation, and on its own premise. The seed
encoding grounded a single "Catholic/Orthodox" line on magisterial
infallibility, which attributes to Orthodoxy a premise it does not hold.

```lean
theorem orthodox_not_establishes : ¬Establishes orthodox
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

#### The three objections, each valid on its own grounds

<a id="selfRefutation_is_valid"></a>
**`selfRefutation_is_valid`**

The self-refutation objection is valid: granted that only scriptural
doctrine binds and that scripture does not teach sola scriptura, the position
fails by its own standard.

```lean
theorem selfRefutation_is_valid : Establishes selfRefutation
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="canonObjection_is_valid"></a>
**`canonObjection_is_valid`**

The canon objection is valid on its own grounds: if the canon is known
through the Church's reception and identifying it requires an infallible
authority, then an authority outside scripture is needed to identify
scripture.

```lean
theorem canonObjection_is_valid : Establishes canonObjection
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="interpretiveRegress_is_valid"></a>
**`interpretiveRegress_is_valid`**

The interpretive-authority regress is valid on its own grounds. It attacks
something the other two do not: not whether the doctrine is scriptural or
whether the canon can be identified, but whether the authority Tradition I
submits to is anything other than the one submitting.

```lean
theorem interpretiveRegress_is_valid : Establishes interpretiveRegress
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

#### The hinge, in its two roles

`solaScripturaIsTaughtByScripture` does two jobs, and they come apart. It is
not load-bearing for reaching the conclusion, because the eliminative line
reaches it without the hinge. It is load-bearing within the classical strand,
and — the result that matters — it is one of only two things that answer the
self-refutation objection.

<a id="hinge_not_load_bearing_for_conclusion"></a>
**`hinge_not_load_bearing_for_conclusion`**

**The hinge is not load-bearing for the conclusion.** Strip it and the
eliminative line still delivers the sole rule, and so does Mark 7's — each on a
premise of its own that the classical line does not need.

```lean
theorem hinge_not_load_bearing_for_conclusion : Establishes
    protestantWithoutHinge
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="hingeDeniedReading"></a>
**`hingeDeniedReading`**

The reading on which scripture does not teach the principle, and the sole
rule does not follow.

```lean
def hingeDeniedReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.solaScripturaIsTaughtByScripture => False
    | Claim.scriptureIsSoleInfallibleRule => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="hinge_is_load_bearing_within_classical_strand"></a>
**`hinge_is_load_bearing_within_classical_strand`**

Within the classical strand taken alone the hinge is still load-bearing:
remove it and that strand yields nothing.

```lean
theorem hinge_is_load_bearing_within_classical_strand : ¬Establishes
    classicalStrandWithoutHinge
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

#### The two answers to self-refutation

The objection's step is a conjunction, so there are two ways to deny it. The
seed encoded only the first. Neither answer is redundant with the other: each
removes a different ground, and the objection succeeds only if both are
refused.

<a id="scriptureTeachesItReading"></a>
**`scriptureTeachesItReading`**

The reading on which scripture does teach the principle.

```lean
def scriptureTeachesItReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun x => True
```

<a id="classical_answer_blocks_self_refutation"></a>
**`classical_answer_blocks_self_refutation`**

**The classical answer blocks the objection.** Assert that scripture teaches
the principle and the objection no longer delivers its denial.

```lean
theorem classical_answer_blocks_self_refutation : ¬Establishes
    selfRefutationAnswered
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="finalArbiterReading"></a>
**`finalArbiterReading`**

The final-arbiter reading: scripture adjudicates doctrine rather than
sourcing every binding claim, so the bindingness rule does not apply reflexively
to a claim about where doctrine comes from.

```lean
def finalArbiterReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.onlyScripturalDoctrineIsBinding => False
    | Claim.solaScripturaIsTaughtByScripture => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="scoping_blocks_self_refutation"></a>
**`scoping_blocks_self_refutation`**

**And the final-arbiter answer blocks it too, without the hinge.** This is
the answer the seed did not encode. It concedes that scripture does not teach
the principle in the sense the objection requires, and denies instead that the
bindingness rule governs a claim of this kind.

So the objection is defeated on either route, and succeeds only against a
position that refuses both — which is what "the dispute reduces to the hinge"
was gesturing at, and is narrower than that phrase suggests.

```lean
theorem scoping_blocks_self_refutation : ¬Establishes selfRefutationUnderScope
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

#### The parity replies, and what they are worth

Kruger on the canon and Mathison on interpretive authority make the same move:
concede the circularity, deny that it discriminates between the positions.

Each used to get two results — one that it blocks the objection, one that it
establishes nothing — and that is one result too many. A premise set that
entails neither a proposition nor its negation leaves that proposition
*independent* of it, and blocking and establishing-nothing are the two halves
of that single fact. Foundation names the notion for provability;
`Testimony.Logic.Independent` is its semantic counterpart, and `leaves_open`
proves it from the two readings the premises admit.

The gain is not brevity. Stated as a pair, nothing checks that the two halves
are about the same proposition — and in the Geisler case below they were
not.

<a id="parityEstablishesNothingReading"></a>
**`parityEstablishesNothingReading`**

The reading on which the parity point is granted and the sole rule still
does not follow: the canon came through the Church, the rival's authority is
self-authenticating too, and scripture is not the sole infallible rule.

```lean
def parityEstablishesNothingReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.scriptureIsSoleInfallibleRule => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="krugerParityReading"></a>
**`krugerParityReading`**

Kruger's reading: the canon's reception is conceded, and the demand for an
infallible identifying authority is refused, because the rival's own authority
is self-authenticating too.

```lean
def krugerParityReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.identifyingCanonRequiresInfallibleAuthority => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="parity_leaves_the_canon_open"></a>
**`parity_leaves_the_canon_open`**

**The parity reply leaves the canon question open.** Granted Kruger's
grounds, the sole infallible rule neither follows nor fails: his own reading
has it, and the reading on which the parity point is conceded and the sole rule
still denied has it not. Both satisfy every premise.

That is the whole of what the reply achieves, in one claim. It blocks the canon
objection — the objection's denial is no longer entailed — and it establishes
nothing, because the conclusion is not entailed either. The parity move is
purely defensive, and this is the form that says so without saying it twice.

```lean
theorem parity_leaves_the_canon_open : Independent canonUnderParity.premises
    (p Claim.scriptureIsSoleInfallibleRule)
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="distinctionUnestablishedReading"></a>
**`distinctionUnestablishedReading`**

The reading on which the parity point is granted and the distinction still
does not follow: tradition is ministerial, choosing an authority is private
judgement, and sola scriptura does not differ in principle from solo
scriptura.

```lean
def distinctionUnestablishedReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.traditionIDiffersInPrincipleFromTradition0 => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="mathisonParityReading"></a>
**`mathisonParityReading`**

Mathison's reading: ministerial authority is retained, and the claim that
the individual keeps ultimate interpretive authority is refused, because
choosing Rome is itself an act of private judgement.

```lean
def mathisonParityReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.individualRetainsUltimateInterpretiveAuthority =>
      False
    | x => True
```

<a id="parity_leaves_the_distinction_open"></a>
**`parity_leaves_the_distinction_open`**

**And the same for interpretive authority.** That choosing an authority is
itself private judgement defeats the charge that Tradition I collapses into
Tradition 0; it does not show that Tradition I differs from it in principle.
Both readings satisfy Mathison's grounds, so his grounds settle the question
neither way.

The same shape, twice, against two different objections — which is the point.
It is a property of the move, not of the objection it answers.

```lean
theorem parity_leaves_the_distinction_open : Independent
    regressUnderParity.premises (p
    Claim.traditionIDiffersInPrincipleFromTradition0)
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

#### Geisler's circle

<a id="neitherEndReading"></a>
**`neitherEndReading`**

The reading on which neither the consensus nor the clarity it is said to
rest on obtains.

```lean
def neitherEndReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.creedalConsensusIsHermeneuticallyNecessary => False
    | Claim.scriptureIsPerspicuous => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="bothEndsHoldReading"></a>
**`bothEndsHoldReading`**

The reading on which both ends of the circle obtain: the consensus is
hermeneutically necessary and scripture is clear. A cycle of implications is
satisfied by this as readily as by the reading on which every node is false,
which is what it means for the cycle to settle nothing.

```lean
def bothEndsHoldReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun x => True
```

<a id="circle_leaves_the_consensus_open"></a>
**`circle_leaves_the_consensus_open`**

**Geisler's circularity charge against Tradition I, shown rather than
alleged.** The creedal consensus is said to rest on scripture's clarity, and
scripture's clear sense is said to be unobtainable without that consensus. Put
both legs in place and the consensus is left *independent* of them: it does not
follow, and neither does its denial.

A cycle of implications is satisfied outright by a valuation on which every
node in it is false, and equally by one on which every node is true. Nothing
enters such a loop from outside, so nothing comes out of it — in either
direction. That second direction is what this result gained when it stopped
being a bare `¬ Establishes`: a circle is not merely silent about whether its
nodes hold, it is silent about whether they fail.

Like every result here this is conditional: deny either leg and the circle is
not there. What it settles is that the charge is structural rather than
rhetorical — and it is made from inside Protestantism, against the position
this module encodes as the Protestant one.

```lean
theorem circle_leaves_the_consensus_open : Independent
    traditionICircle.premises (p
    Claim.creedalConsensusIsHermeneuticallyNecessary)
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="circle_leaves_the_perspicuity_open"></a>
**`circle_leaves_the_perspicuity_open`**

**And the other end is no better off.** The same two legs, asked about
perspicuity instead of the consensus, leave it open in the same way and on the
same two readings.

Both results are needed, and they are not two halves of one claim: a circle has
two ends, and each is a separate proposition the premises fail to settle. What
*is* one claim is each result's own two directions, which is why each is an
`Independent` rather than a pair.

```lean
theorem circle_leaves_the_perspicuity_open : Independent
    traditionICircle.premises (p Claim.scriptureIsPerspicuous)
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

#### Geisler's charge, and the three replies

The cycle results above are a formal fact about a cycle of implications. These
are about the charge as an argument: whether it goes through, and what answers
it. Two replies deny its second leg; Barrett's concedes the circle and denies
that circularity is peculiar to this position.

<a id="geislerCircle_is_valid"></a>
**`geislerCircle_is_valid`**

Geisler's charge is valid on its own grounds: grant that the consensus
rests on scripture's clarity and that scripture's clear sense requires the
consensus, and the reasoning is circular.

```lean
theorem geislerCircle_is_valid : Establishes geislerCircle
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="accountabilityReading"></a>
**`accountabilityReading`**

The reading on which the consensus is a product of scripture rather than a
precondition of reading it.

```lean
def accountabilityReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.perspicuityRequiresCreedalConsensus => False
    | Claim.traditionIReasoningIsCircular => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="accountability_blocks_the_circle"></a>
**`accountability_blocks_the_circle`**

**Allen and Swain's reply blocks the charge.** If the creedal consensus is
established by and accountable to scripture, it is what reading scripture
produces rather than what reading scripture presupposes, and the second leg
fails.

What this costs is worth stating: Geisler quotes Mathison saying that it is "to
the Church that we must turn for the true interpretation of the Scripture" and
that without the early rule of faith "hermeneutical chaos and anarchy" reigns.
If that is Tradition I, the reply defends a weaker position than the one
charged.

```lean
theorem accountability_blocks_the_circle : ¬Establishes
    geislerCircleUnderAccountability
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="scripturallyBoundedOfficeReading"></a>
**`scripturallyBoundedOfficeReading`**

The reading on which scripture bounds the interpretive office, and
perspicuity is claimed only for salvation essentials.

```lean
def scripturallyBoundedOfficeReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.perspicuityRequiresCreedalConsensus => False
    | Claim.traditionIReasoningIsCircular => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="scripturalBounding_blocks_the_circle"></a>
**`scripturalBounding_blocks_the_circle`** ⚗

**The scriptural-bounding reply blocks the charge too, and on scriptural
rather than confessional grounds.**

**What is novel here.** No source was found advancing these texts as an answer
to the circularity charge; the passages are cited and the use is assembled in
this library. Acts 20:32 commends the Ephesian elders to "the word of his
grace" rather than to their own office; Titus 1:9 constitutes the office by
holding to "the trustworthy word as taught"; 1 Peter 5:2–3 forbids domineering.
If scripture bounds the interpretive office, the consensus's own warrant is
read off scripture, so it cannot be a precondition of reading scripture — and
Westminster I.7 restricts the perspicuity claim to what is necessary for
salvation, which is not the set of boundaries the creeds fix.

**What would settle whether it is really new.** Mark Thompson's *A Clear and
Present Word* treats the church-as-interpreter objection at length and was not
available here; Vanhoozer's *Biblical Authority after Babel* covers the same
ground. Either may already make this argument, in which case this result should
be recited to them and the tag dropped.

**What it deliberately does not claim.** That scripture *confers* the office.
Conferral invites the recognition/conferral distinction Mathison presses
against Rome over the canon, and boundedness is all the reply needs. It also
does not escape the regress: a critic may say the texts are read this way
because of a tradition. It moves the dispute to far less contested ground; it
does not leave it.

```lean
theorem scripturalBounding_blocks_the_circle : ¬Establishes
    geislerCircleUnderScripturalBounding
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="universalCircularityReading"></a>
**`universalCircularityReading`**

Barrett's own reading: the circle is granted, it is granted to be
universal, and so it does not defeat this position in particular.

```lean
def universalCircularityReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.circularityDefeatsTraditionI => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="universalityDoesNotAcquitReading"></a>
**`universalityDoesNotAcquitReading`**

The sceptic's reading of the same grounds: the circle is granted and its
universality is granted, and the defeat lands anyway. That every ultimate
authority reasons in a circle is read as a charge against all of them rather
than an acquittal of any — including Tradition I.

```lean
def universalityDoesNotAcquitReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun x => True
```

<a id="parity_leaves_the_defeat_open"></a>
**`parity_leaves_the_defeat_open`**

**Barrett's parity reply leaves the defeat open.** Concede the circle; deny
that it is a defect peculiar to this position, since any appeal to an ultimate
authority is circular. On his grounds the defeat does not follow — and neither
does its failure, because the same grounds are satisfied by the reading on
which universal circularity convicts everyone rather than excusing anyone.

The sixth instance of one move. Kruger on the canon, Mathison on interpretive
authority, Athanasius on ὁμοούσιος, Whitaker on unwritten tradition, Geisler
himself on who may interpret the Old Testament, and now Barrett on perspicuity
— against Geisler, who deploys it himself elsewhere.

**This result is not what it was.** It stood as half of a pair whose other half
asked a *different question of the same premises* — whether the reply clears
the charge of circularity, not whether it blocks the defeat — and the pair was
presented as though the two were complements. Naming the shape exposed that:
an independence claim has to say which proposition is left open, and only one
of the two could be named.

```lean
theorem parity_leaves_the_defeat_open : Independent defeatUnderParity.premises
    (p Claim.circularityDefeatsTraditionI)
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="circle_parity_concedes_the_charge"></a>
**`circle_parity_concedes_the_charge`**

**The reply does not merely fail to clear the charge — it grants it.** This
is the second question, kept because it is worth asking and restated because
the answer is stronger than "establishes nothing". Barrett's grounds include
`traditionIReasoningIsCircular` outright: what the parity move denies is that
the circularity is damaging, not that it is there. A position defended only by
this reply is circular and keeping company, and that now follows from the
reply's own premises rather than from the failure of a rival reading.

```lean
theorem circle_parity_concedes_the_charge : Establishes
    circleParityConcedingTheCharge
-- axioms: propext
```

#### Refusing a ground, and denying it

Every reply above is written the same way, as the objection's own line with a
ground replaced. That shape covers two different moves. A reply can **deny** the
ground — entail its negation — or merely **refuse** it, declining to grant it
without asserting the opposite. A denial is an *attack*, and in a dispute an
attack can defeat (`Testimony.Logic.Dispute`). A refusal attacks nothing: it
takes the ground away, which is what `Line.onGrounds` encodes, and the question
it leaves is an entailment question the results above already answer.

Five of the seven replies here refuse. Each refusal is shown by a reading that
grants the reply's grounds and keeps the refused ground true. The other two
deny, and each denial is an entailment.

<a id="kruger_refuses_rather_than_denies"></a>
**`kruger_refuses_rather_than_denies`**

**Kruger refuses the canon objection's ground; he does not deny it.** On
the reading that grants his grounds and still denies the sole rule, identifying
the canon does require an infallible authority.

```lean
theorem kruger_refuses_rather_than_denies : ¬Entails canonUnderParity.premises
    (∼p Claim.identifyingCanonRequiresInfallibleAuthority)
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="mathison_refuses_rather_than_denies"></a>
**`mathison_refuses_rather_than_denies`**

**Mathison refuses the regress's ground.** Granted his grounds, the
individual may still retain ultimate interpretive authority.

```lean
theorem mathison_refuses_rather_than_denies : ¬Entails
    regressUnderParity.premises (∼p
    Claim.individualRetainsUltimateInterpretiveAuthority)
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="final_arbiter_refuses_rather_than_denies"></a>
**`final_arbiter_refuses_rather_than_denies`**

**The final-arbiter answer refuses the self-refutation objection's ground.**
Scoping the bindingness rule to first-order doctrine does not deny that only
scriptural doctrine binds.

```lean
theorem final_arbiter_refuses_rather_than_denies : ¬Entails
    selfRefutationUnderFinalArbiter.premises (∼p
    Claim.onlyScripturalDoctrineIsBinding)
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="accountability_refuses_rather_than_denies"></a>
**`accountability_refuses_rather_than_denies`**

**Allen and Swain refuse the circle's second leg.** A consensus accountable
to scripture does not, by itself, deny that perspicuity requires the
consensus.

```lean
theorem accountability_refuses_rather_than_denies : ¬Entails
    circleUnderAccountability.premises (∼p
    Claim.perspicuityRequiresCreedalConsensus)
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="scriptural_bounding_refuses_rather_than_denies"></a>
**`scriptural_bounding_refuses_rather_than_denies`**

**The scriptural-bounding reply refuses the same leg.**

```lean
theorem scriptural_bounding_refuses_rather_than_denies : ¬Entails
    circleUnderScripturalBounding.premises (∼p
    Claim.perspicuityRequiresCreedalConsensus)
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="classical_answer_denies_the_ground"></a>
**`classical_answer_denies_the_ground`**

**The classical answer denies the self-refutation objection's ground.** It
asserts that scripture teaches the principle, which is the negation of what the
objection assumes.

```lean
theorem classical_answer_denies_the_ground : Entails
    selfRefutationUnderClassicalAnswer.premises (∼notP
    Claim.solaScripturaIsTaughtByScripture)
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="barrett_denies_the_ground"></a>
**`barrett_denies_the_ground`**

**Barrett denies the ground Geisler's charge needs.** He asserts that every
appeal to an ultimate authority is circular, the negation of what the charge
assumes.

```lean
theorem barrett_denies_the_ground : Entails defeatUnderParity.premises (∼notP
    Claim.everyUltimateAuthorityIsCircular)
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

#### Satisfiability

`Entails` quantifies over the valuations satisfying the premises, so a premise
set with no model entails everything — including the negation of what its own
author intended. A package built from contradictory premises would `Establishes`
its conclusion, the proof would close, and every gate would pass.

Only packages carrying a positive `Establishes` result need checking here. A
package with a `¬ Establishes` result is satisfiable already: its countermodel
is a valuation on which every premise holds.

These are not tagged `@[headline]`. They are claims about the health of the
encoding, not about the dispute.

<a id="everythingHoldsReading"></a>
**`everythingHoldsReading`**

The reading on which every claim in this argument holds at once. Not a
position anyone occupies — it is the witness that the packages built only from
positive grounds are coherent.

```lean
def everythingHoldsReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun x => True
```

<a id="protestantReading"></a>
**`protestantReading`**

The Protestant reading: every claim in this argument holds but two, that a
general council after the apostles binds with the Spirit's authority and cannot
err, and that those who hold the Church's teaching office are heeded for the
seat they hold. The Protestant packages read Acts 15 and Moses' seat as the
Reformers did, and deny both.

```lean
def protestantReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.councilBindsWithTheSpiritsAuthority => False
    | Claim.teachingOfficeHeardByItsSeat => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="protestant_is_satisfiable"></a>
**`protestant_is_satisfiable`**

The Protestant package has a model, so `protestant_establishes` is not
vacuous.

```lean
theorem protestant_is_satisfiable : Satisfiable protestant.premises
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="tradition0_is_satisfiable"></a>
**`tradition0_is_satisfiable`**

Tradition 0's package has a model.

```lean
theorem tradition0_is_satisfiable : Satisfiable tradition0.premises
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="protestantWithoutHinge_is_satisfiable"></a>
**`protestantWithoutHinge_is_satisfiable`**

The Protestant package minus the hinge has a model, so
`hinge_not_load_bearing_for_conclusion` is not vacuous either — which matters,
since a load-bearing result that held only because its premises were
contradictory would be precisely backwards.

```lean
theorem protestantWithoutHinge_is_satisfiable : Satisfiable
    protestantWithoutHinge.premises
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="geislerCircle_is_satisfiable"></a>
**`geislerCircle_is_satisfiable`**

Geisler's charge has a model.

```lean
theorem geislerCircle_is_satisfiable : Satisfiable geislerCircle.premises
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="circleParityConcedingTheCharge_is_satisfiable"></a>
**`circleParityConcedingTheCharge_is_satisfiable`**

Barrett's parity grounds have a model — the sceptic's reading, which grants
the circle, grants its universality, and lets the defeat land.

```lean
theorem circleParityConcedingTheCharge_is_satisfiable : Satisfiable
    circleParityConcedingTheCharge.premises
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="selfRefutationOwnReading"></a>
**`selfRefutationOwnReading`**

The world the self-refutation objection describes: scripture does not teach
the principle, so the sole rule does not bind.

```lean
def selfRefutationOwnReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.solaScripturaIsTaughtByScripture => False
    | Claim.scriptureIsSoleInfallibleRule => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="selfRefutation_is_satisfiable"></a>
**`selfRefutation_is_satisfiable`**

The self-refutation objection has a model.

```lean
theorem selfRefutation_is_satisfiable : Satisfiable selfRefutation.premises
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="canonObjectionOwnReading"></a>
**`canonObjectionOwnReading`**

The world the canon objection describes: the canon comes through the
Church, so scripture is not the sole infallible rule.

```lean
def canonObjectionOwnReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.scriptureIsSoleInfallibleRule => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="canonObjection_is_satisfiable"></a>
**`canonObjection_is_satisfiable`**

The canon objection has a model.

```lean

-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="interpretiveRegressOwnReading"></a>
**`interpretiveRegressOwnReading`**

The world the regress describes: sola scriptura does not differ in

```lean
def interpretiveRegressOwnReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.traditionIDiffersInPrincipleFromTradition0 => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="interpretiveRegress_is_satisfiable"></a>
**`interpretiveRegress_is_satisfiable`**

The interpretive-authority regress has a model.

```lean
theorem interpretiveRegress_is_satisfiable : Satisfiable
    interpretiveRegress.premises
```

## TestimonyArguments.SolaScriptura.Mark7 — what Jesus' rebuke of tradition settles

The Pharisees and scribes ask why Jesus' disciples eat with unwashed hands,
against "the tradition of the elders". Jesus answers with Isaiah 29:13 — "in
vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men" — and
with Corban: a gift vowed to God releases a son from supporting his father and
mother, "thus making void the word of God by your tradition" (Mark 7:1–13;
Matthew 15:1–9). The Protestant case has always cited it, and here it is a line
of reason of its own.

### What Mark 7 settles

**The principle is common ground.** God's word judges human tradition: no
commandment of men may be taught as God's word, and a tradition that voids
God's command is void. Rome says the same — its teaching office is "not above
the word of God" (*Dei Verbum* 10) — and so the principle is not a Protestant
win. Trent, as it states its position, can hold every word of it
(`trent_grants_marks_principle`).

**It does not reach sola scriptura on its own.** From the principle to "Scripture
is the sole infallible rule" needs one more premise: that no unwritten tradition
can now be shown to be apostolic, so that none can bind the conscience as God's
word. That is William Whitaker's claim against Bellarmine in 1588, and it is a
claim about proof, not about what the apostles once said: "the papists have no
such unwritten tradition which can be certainly shewn to have been always
observed by the universal church". Without it, Mark 7 leaves the sole rule open —
neither it nor its denial follows
(`mark7_without_the_hinge_leaves_the_sole_rule_open`). With it, the conclusion
follows (`mark7Case_establishes`), and the premise is rated `disputed`. Rome
denies it: Trent says the gospel's truth and discipline "are contained in the
written books, and the unwritten traditions", and *Dei Verbum* 9 says that "it is not from Sacred
Scripture alone that the Church draws her certainty about everything which has
been revealed". The step itself is disputed too. A reader can grant the
principle, and grant that no unwritten tradition can be shown to be apostolic,
and still deny that Scripture is the *sole* infallible rule: Florovsky, for whom
tradition adds nothing to Scripture and the mind of the Church interprets it; or
a Catholic who holds Scripture materially sufficient and the Magisterium
infallible.

Mark 7 is not the only text for the principle. Jesus' sayings in John 10:35 and
Matthew 5:18, and Paul's in Galatians 1:8–9 and Colossians 2:8, 20–22, deliver
it too, and without that premise they leave the sole rule just as open
(`JesusAndPaul.lean`).

### What Rome's "tradition" means

The question the passage raises for a reader is whether the tradition Jesus
condemns is the thing Rome means by Tradition. `whatTrentsTraditionIs` answers
both readings.

- **Read as commandments of men** — Calvin's reading of the laws of worship he
  opposed, applying Matthew 15:9 to them (*Institutes* IV.x.23) — Trent's claim
  is exactly what Mark 7 condemns. The reading cannot be held with Mark 7's
  principle, at a step rated `wellSupported`.
- **Read as the apostolic word handed on unwritten** — what Trent says it
  receives, traditions "received by the Apostles from the mouth of Christ
  himself, or from the Apostles themselves, the Holy Ghost dictating" (Session
  IV, in Waterworth's translation) — Mark 7 does not reach it. Nothing in the principle is denied.
  The reading meets the Mark 7 case only at the premise the step to sola
  scriptura needs, that no unwritten tradition can be shown to be apostolic,
  and that premise is `disputed`.

So Mark 7 does not decide between Rome and the Reformers. It moves the question
to what the sola scriptura argument already turned on: whether any unwritten
tradition can be shown to be apostolic — and, even granting that none can,
whether the principle then makes Scripture the *sole* infallible rule.

#### The quotation

<a id="mark7QuotesIsaiah"></a>
**`mark7QuotesIsaiah`**

**Mark 7:6–7 quotes Isaiah 29:13.** Typed `.quotation`, not `.allusion`:
Jesus introduces the words with "as it is written", and Mark gives them close to
the Septuagint's wording.

```lean
def mark7QuotesIsaiah : IntertextEdge :=
  { fromPassage := Scripture.mark7_7, toPassage := Scripture.isaiah29_13,
    relation := RelationType.quotation,
    source := Scripture.na28Apparatus Scripture.mark7_7 }
```

<a id="matthew15QuotesIsaiah"></a>
**`matthew15QuotesIsaiah`**

**Matthew 15:8–9 quotes the same verse**, in the parallel account.

```lean
def matthew15QuotesIsaiah : IntertextEdge :=
  { fromPassage := Scripture.matthew15_9, toPassage := Scripture.isaiah29_13,
    relation := RelationType.quotation,
    source := Scripture.na28Apparatus Scripture.matthew15_9 }
```

#### The positions

<a id="mark7Principle"></a>
**`mark7Principle`** — Mark 7: God's word judges human tradition

**Mark 7's principle**: Jesus' rebuke of the elders' tradition, and what it
enacts — God's word judges human tradition, and no commandment of men is to be
taught as God's word. It concludes the principle, and claims nothing about
Scripture's place among the rules of faith.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{#claim-3}{P_{3}}\\) — Mark 7:1–13 (Matthew 15:1–9) — Jesus rebukes the elders' tradition, Corban above all, for voiding God's command
- (2) \\(\href{#claim-3}{P_{3}} \rightarrow \href{#claim-37}{P_{37}}\\)
- (3) \\(\href{#claim-37}{P_{37}} \rightarrow \lnot \href{#claim-38}{P_{38}}\\) — *would deny:* A commandment of men may rightly be bound on the Church as God's word
- \\(\vdash\\) \\(\href{#claim-37}{P_{37}}\\) — *at issue:* God's word judges human tradition: no commandment of men may be taught as God's word, and a tradition that voids God's command is void

</div>

No premise here rests on scripture alone.

<a id="mark7Case"></a>
**`mark7Case`** — Sola scriptura from Mark 7

**Mark 7's case for sola scriptura**: the principle, and the premise that no
unwritten tradition can now be shown to be apostolic.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{#claim-3}{P_{3}}\\) — Mark 7:1–13 (Matthew 15:1–9) — Jesus rebukes the elders' tradition, Corban above all, for voiding God's command
- (2) \\(\href{#claim-39}{P_{39}}\\) — No unwritten tradition can now be shown to be apostolic, so none can bind the conscience as the word of God
- (3) \\(\href{#claim-3}{P_{3}} \rightarrow \href{#claim-37}{P_{37}}\\) — *would give:* God's word judges human tradition: no commandment of men may be taught as God's word, and a tradition that voids God's command is void
- (4) \\((\href{#claim-37}{P_{37}} \land \href{#claim-39}{P_{39}}) \rightarrow \href{#claim-9}{P_{9}}\\)
- \\(\vdash\\) \\(\href{#claim-9}{P_{9}}\\) — *at issue:* Scripture is the sole infallible rule of faith

</div>

No premise here rests on scripture alone.

<a id="mark7CaseWithoutTheHinge"></a>
**`mark7CaseWithoutTheHinge`** — Sola scriptura from Mark 7, without the premise about unwritten tradition

Mark 7's case without the premise that no unwritten tradition can now be
shown to be apostolic: the text, the principle, and the step to the sole
rule.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{#claim-3}{P_{3}}\\) — Mark 7:1–13 (Matthew 15:1–9) — Jesus rebukes the elders' tradition, Corban above all, for voiding God's command
- (2) \\(\href{#claim-3}{P_{3}} \rightarrow \href{#claim-37}{P_{37}}\\) — *would give:* God's word judges human tradition: no commandment of men may be taught as God's word, and a tradition that voids God's command is void
- (3) \\((\href{#claim-37}{P_{37}} \land \href{#claim-39}{P_{39}}) \rightarrow \href{#claim-9}{P_{9}}\\)
- \\(\vdash\\) \\(\href{#claim-9}{P_{9}}\\) — *at issue:* Scripture is the sole infallible rule of faith

</div>

No premise here rests on scripture alone.

<a id="tridentineCase"></a>
**`tridentineCase`** — Trent (Tradition II)

**Trent (Tradition II)**, as Mathison reads it: 2 Thessalonians 2:15 and
tradition as a source of revelation alongside Scripture, so Scripture is not the
sole rule. Unread: it says what Trent receives, not whether it is apostolic word
or a commandment of men. The package `tridentine` asks these premises whether
sola scriptura follows; this one states what they conclude, which is what a
dispute weighs.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{#claim-5}{P_{5}}\\) — 2 Thessalonians 2:15 — hold to the traditions taught by word or letter
- (2) \\(\href{#claim-13}{P_{13}}\\) — Tradition is a coordinate source of revelation alongside scripture
- (3) \\((\href{#claim-5}{P_{5}} \land \href{#claim-13}{P_{13}}) \rightarrow \lnot \href{#claim-9}{P_{9}}\\)
- \\(\vdash\\) \\(\lnot \href{#claim-9}{P_{9}}\\) — *at issue, the denial of:* Scripture is the sole infallible rule of faith

</div>

Grounded in scripture alone: 2 Thessalonians 2:15 — hold to the traditions taught by word or letter.

#### Two readings of Trent's "tradition"

<a id="trentReadAsMensCommandments"></a>
**`trentReadAsMensCommandments`**

Reading Trent's traditions as commandments of men: God "is worshipped with
laws of human invention", Calvin says of the laws of worship he opposed, and he
applies Matthew 15:9 to them — "in vain do they worship me, teaching for
doctrines the commandments of men" (*Institutes* IV.x.23). Rated `disputed`:
Trent, *Dei Verbum* 9–10 and the *Catechism* deny that what Trent receives is of
human origin — the *Catechism* (§83) distinguishes the apostolic Tradition from
the "theological, disciplinary, liturgical or devotional traditions" which "can
be retained, modified or even abandoned". No one reads Trent as *claiming* human
origin: this is a reading of what those traditions are, not of what Trent
says.

```lean
def trentReadAsMensCommandments : Source :=
  {
    primary :=
      Reference.work Bib.calvinInstitutes (Bib.Locus.sectionRef "IV.x.23"),
    tradition := Tradition.reformedProtestant,
    confidence := Confidence.disputed }
```

<a id="trentReadAsApostolicWord"></a>
**`trentReadAsApostolicWord`**

Reading Trent's traditions as the apostolic word handed on unwritten: what
Trent says it receives, the traditions "received by the Apostles from the mouth
of Christ himself, or from the Apostles themselves, the Holy Ghost dictating"
(Session IV, Waterworth 18). *Dei Verbum* 9 says the same: tradition "takes the
word of God entrusted by Christ the Lord and the Holy Spirit to the Apostles,
and hands it on". Rated `consensus` as an account of what Trent claims: Calvin
and Chemnitz do not deny that Trent claims apostolic origin; they deny that the
claim is true.

```lean
def trentReadAsApostolicWord : Source :=
  { primary := Reference.work waterworthTrent (Bib.Locus.page 18),
    supporting :=
      [Reference.work tannerDecrees
          (Bib.Locus.sectionRef
            "Trent, Session IV (1546), Decree on Sacred Books and Traditions"),
        Reference.work tannerDecrees
          (Bib.Locus.sectionRef "Vatican II (1965), Dei Verbum 9"),
        Reference.work catechismCatholicChurch (Bib.Locus.sectionRef "83")],
    tradition := Tradition.romanCatholic, confidence := Confidence.consensus }
```


#### Readings, written down

<a id="marksPrincipleReading"></a>
**`marksPrincipleReading`**

The Reformed world: Mark 7's text and principle, no commandment of men bound
as God's word, no unwritten tradition shown to be apostolic, and sola
scriptura.

```lean
def marksPrincipleReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.mensCommandmentBindsAsGodsWord => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="romeGrantsMarksPrincipleReading"></a>
**`romeGrantsMarksPrincipleReading`**

Rome's world, granting Mark 7: God's word judges human tradition and no
commandment of men may be bound as God's word; but unwritten tradition is known
to be apostolic and binds as God's word, so Scripture is not the sole infallible rule. Nor is the
Church's consensus a mere product of reading Scripture: for Rome, Scripture and
Tradition flow from one source (*Dei Verbum* 9). A world must choose here,
because the meanings exclude the consensus being that product and its being
needed for Scripture's clear sense (`TestimonyArguments.Meanings.SolaScriptura.joins`).
And the apostles' office did not end with them: bishops succeed to it (*Lumen
Gentium* 20).

```lean
def romeGrantsMarksPrincipleReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.apostlesOfficeEndedWithThem => False
    | Claim.creedalConsensusIsDerivedFromScripture => False
    | Claim.mensCommandmentBindsAsGodsWord => False
    | Claim.noUnwrittenTraditionShownApostolic => False
    | Claim.scriptureIsSoleInfallibleRule => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="mensCommandmentsReading"></a>
**`mensCommandmentsReading`**

A world in which Trent, its tradition read Calvin's way, holds together: its
tradition is a commandment of men bound as God's word, and Scripture is not the
sole rule. It must give up Mark 7's principle, so no one holds this world; it
shows only that the reading is coherent on its own.

```lean
def mensCommandmentsReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.godsWordJudgesTradition => False
    | Claim.scriptureIsSoleInfallibleRule => False
    | x => True
```

#### Mark 7's principle, and what it reaches

<a id="mark7Principle_establishes"></a>


**Trent grants Mark 7's principle.** Trent's position, as it states it, can
be held with the principle and everything Mark 7 says: the reading on which

```lean
theorem trent_grants_marks_principle : Grants tridentineCase (p
```

<a id="mark7Case_establishes"></a>

```lean
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="mark7Case_is_satisfiable"></a>
**`mark7Case_is_satisfiable`**

Mark 7's case can be held without contradiction.

```lean

-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="mark7_without_the_hinge_leaves_the_sole_rule_open"></a>
**`mark7_without_the_hinge_leaves_the_sole_rule_open`**

**Without that premise, Mark 7 leaves the sole rule open.** Grant the text,
the principle, and the step from them to the sole rule: sola scriptura neither
follows nor fails. Rome's reading grants all of it and denies the sole rule;

#### Where each reading breaks

<a id="whereTheMensCommandmentsReadingFalls"></a>
**`whereTheMensCommandmentsReadingFalls`**

**Why Mark 7 stands against Trent, read as commandments of men.** The crux is
what the principle says of a commandment of men: it may not be bound as God's
word. What it breaks is Trent's claim with the reading — tradition
received alongside Scripture, and that tradition a commandment of men. Nothing
else in Trent is touched. The crux is Mark 7's answer to the reading, not part
of its case for the principle, which follows without it.

**Why *Mark 7: God's word judges human tradition* stands against *Trent (Tradition II), read as commandments of men*.**

- **The crux:** \\(\href{#claim-37}{P_{37}} \rightarrow \lnot \href{#claim-38}{P_{38}}\\), a premise of *Mark 7: God's word judges human tradition*.
- **What it does:** its conclusion follows without it — the crux is its answer to *Trent (Tradition II), read as commandments of men*.
- **Granted:** \\(\href{#claim-3}{P_{3}}\\), \\(\href{#claim-3}{P_{3}} \rightarrow \href{#claim-37}{P_{37}}\\), which the break also needs.
- **Where the rival breaks:** \\(\href{#claim-13}{P_{13}}\\), \\(\href{#claim-13}{P_{13}} \rightarrow \href{#claim-38}{P_{38}}\\) cannot be held together with \\(\href{#claim-37}{P_{37}} \rightarrow \lnot \href{#claim-38}{P_{38}}\\) and \\(\href{#claim-3}{P_{3}}\\), \\(\href{#claim-3}{P_{3}} \rightarrow \href{#claim-37}{P_{37}}\\); each is needed for the break, and without the crux they stand.
- **What this rests on:**
  - \\(\href{#claim-3}{P_{3}}\\) Mark 7:1–13 (Matthew 15:1–9) — Jesus rebukes the elders' tradition, Corban above all, for voiding God's command — *consensus*: Mark 7:1-13; Matt 15:1-9; [Calvin 1960](../bibliography.md#calvin-institutes-1960), §IV.x.10
  - \\(\href{#claim-37}{P_{37}}\\) God's word judges human tradition: no commandment of men may be taught as God's word, and a tradition that voids God's command is void — *consensus*: [Tanner 1990](../bibliography.md#tanner-decrees-1990), §Vatican II (1965), Dei Verbum 10; [Calvin 1960](../bibliography.md#calvin-institutes-1960), §IV.x.23; [Florovsky 1972](../bibliography.md#florovsky-bible-church-tradition-1972)
  - the step itself — *well supported*: [Tanner 1990](../bibliography.md#tanner-decrees-1990), §Vatican II (1965), Dei Verbum 10; [Calvin 1960](../bibliography.md#calvin-institutes-1960), §IV.x.23; [Wenham 1953](../bibliography.md#wenham-our-lords-view-1953), pp. 15–16

<a id="whereTheApostolicWordReadingFalls"></a>
**`whereTheApostolicWordReadingFalls`**

**Why Mark 7's case stands against Trent, read as the apostolic word.** Not
at the principle, which this reading grants, but at the premise the step to
sola scriptura needs: that no unwritten tradition can be shown to be apostolic.
The reading denies exactly that, and the premise is rated `disputed`. The step
from it to the sole rule is `disputed` too, so granting the premise would not
alone settle the question.

**Why *Sola scriptura from Mark 7* stands against *Trent (Tradition II), read as the apostolic word handed on unwritten*.**

- **The crux:** \\(\href{#claim-39}{P_{39}}\\), a premise of *Sola scriptura from Mark 7*.
- **What it does:** its conclusion does not follow without it.
- **Where the rival breaks:** \\(\href{#claim-13}{P_{13}}\\), \\(\href{#claim-13}{P_{13}} \rightarrow \lnot \href{#claim-39}{P_{39}}\\) cannot be held together with \\(\href{#claim-39}{P_{39}}\\); each is needed for the break, and without the crux they stand.
- **What this rests on:**
  - \\(\href{#claim-39}{P_{39}}\\) No unwritten tradition can now be shown to be apostolic, so none can bind the conscience as the word of God — *disputed*: [Whitaker 1849](../bibliography.md#whitaker-disputation-1849), pp. 503–511; [Whitaker 1849](../bibliography.md#whitaker-disputation-1849), p. 594; [Westminster Assembly 1647](../bibliography.md#westminster-confession-1647), §I.6

#### The dilemma

<a id="whatTrentsTraditionIs"></a>
**`whatTrentsTraditionIs`**

**What Trent's tradition is, read both ways.** The claim is Trent's: tradition
is received as a source of revelation alongside Scripture.

Read as commandments of men, it cannot be held with Mark 7's principle, at a
step rated `wellSupported`: Isaiah 29:13, as Jesus quotes it, says a commandment
of men may not be bound as God's word.

Read as the apostolic word handed on unwritten — what Trent says it receives —
Mark 7's principle does not reach it. It cannot be held with Mark 7's case for
sola scriptura, but only at that case's own premise that no unwritten tradition
can be shown to be apostolic, which is `disputed`. That is the question the sola
scriptura argument already turns on; Mark 7 does not settle it.

Each reading is fair: Trent read either way can be held without contradiction. Which reading
fits Trent is not something the dilemma decides; what it shows is what each
costs.

**Every reading of \\(\href{#claim-13}{P_{13}}\\), answered.** *Trent (Tradition II)* holds \\(\href{#claim-13}{P_{13}}\\). It is read 2 ways here, and each reading is checked; none can be left out.

**1. Read as commandments of men.** The claim commits *Trent (Tradition II)* to \\(\href{#claim-38}{P_{38}}\\) — so read by [Calvin 1960](../bibliography.md#calvin-institutes-1960), §IV.x.23 (*disputed*).

Against *Mark 7: God's word judges human tradition*, it cannot be held. Where it breaks:

**Why *Mark 7: God's word judges human tradition* stands against *Trent (Tradition II), read as commandments of men*.**

- **The crux:** \\(\href{#claim-37}{P_{37}} \rightarrow \lnot \href{#claim-38}{P_{38}}\\), a premise of *Mark 7: God's word judges human tradition*.
- **What it does:** its conclusion follows without it — the crux is its answer to *Trent (Tradition II), read as commandments of men*.
- **Granted:** \\(\href{#claim-3}{P_{3}}\\), \\(\href{#claim-3}{P_{3}} \rightarrow \href{#claim-37}{P_{37}}\\), which the break also needs.
- **Where the rival breaks:** \\(\href{#claim-13}{P_{13}}\\), \\(\href{#claim-13}{P_{13}} \rightarrow \href{#claim-38}{P_{38}}\\) cannot be held together with \\(\href{#claim-37}{P_{37}} \rightarrow \lnot \href{#claim-38}{P_{38}}\\) and \\(\href{#claim-3}{P_{3}}\\), \\(\href{#claim-3}{P_{3}} \rightarrow \href{#claim-37}{P_{37}}\\); each is needed for the break, and without the crux they stand.
- **What this rests on:**
  - \\(\href{#claim-3}{P_{3}}\\) Mark 7:1–13 (Matthew 15:1–9) — Jesus rebukes the elders' tradition, Corban above all, for voiding God's command — *consensus*: Mark 7:1-13; Matt 15:1-9; [Calvin 1960](../bibliography.md#calvin-institutes-1960), §IV.x.10
  - \\(\href{#claim-37}{P_{37}}\\) God's word judges human tradition: no commandment of men may be taught as God's word, and a tradition that voids God's command is void — *consensus*: [Tanner 1990](../bibliography.md#tanner-decrees-1990), §Vatican II (1965), Dei Verbum 10; [Calvin 1960](../bibliography.md#calvin-institutes-1960), §IV.x.23; [Florovsky 1972](../bibliography.md#florovsky-bible-church-tradition-1972)
  - the step itself — *well supported*: [Tanner 1990](../bibliography.md#tanner-decrees-1990), §Vatican II (1965), Dei Verbum 10; [Calvin 1960](../bibliography.md#calvin-institutes-1960), §IV.x.23; [Wenham 1953](../bibliography.md#wenham-our-lords-view-1953), pp. 15–16

**2. Read as the apostolic word handed on unwritten.** The claim commits *Trent (Tradition II)* to \\(\lnot \href{#claim-39}{P_{39}}\\) — so read by [Council of Trent 1848](../bibliography.md#waterworth-trent-1848), p. 18; [Tanner 1990](../bibliography.md#tanner-decrees-1990), §Trent, Session IV (1546), Decree on Sacred Books and Traditions; [Tanner 1990](../bibliography.md#tanner-decrees-1990), §Vatican II (1965), Dei Verbum 9; [Catholic Church 2000](../bibliography.md#catholic-church-catechism-2000), §83 (*consensus*).

Against *Mark 7: God's word judges human tradition*, it is not reached: *Mark 7: God's word judges human tradition* holds, and can be held together with it.

Against *Sola scriptura from Mark 7*, it cannot be held. Where it breaks:

**Why *Sola scriptura from Mark 7* stands against *Trent (Tradition II), read as the apostolic word handed on unwritten*.**

- **The crux:** \\(\href{#claim-39}{P_{39}}\\), a premise of *Sola scriptura from Mark 7*.
- **What it does:** its conclusion does not follow without it.
- **Where the rival breaks:** \\(\href{#claim-13}{P_{13}}\\), \\(\href{#claim-13}{P_{13}} \rightarrow \lnot \href{#claim-39}{P_{39}}\\) cannot be held together with \\(\href{#claim-39}{P_{39}}\\); each is needed for the break, and without the crux they stand.
- **What this rests on:**
  - \\(\href{#claim-39}{P_{39}}\\) No unwritten tradition can now be shown to be apostolic, so none can bind the conscience as the word of God — *disputed*: [Whitaker 1849](../bibliography.md#whitaker-disputation-1849), pp. 503–511; [Whitaker 1849](../bibliography.md#whitaker-disputation-1849), p. 594; [Westminster Assembly 1647](../bibliography.md#westminster-confession-1647), §I.6

## TestimonyArguments.SolaScriptura.JesusAndPaul — the same principle, beyond Mark 7

A reader who has followed the case from Mark 7 may fairly ask whether it rests
on one story. It does not. Jesus says elsewhere that "the scripture cannot be
broken" (John 10:35), and that "Till heaven and earth pass, one jot or one
tittle shall in no wise pass from the law, till all be fulfilled" (Matthew
5:18). Paul writes to the Galatians, "though we, or an angel from heaven, preach
any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be
accursed" (Galatians 1:8), and to the Colossians, "Beware lest any man spoil you
through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the
rudiments of the world, and not after Christ" (Colossians 2:8). Of the rules
"Touch not; taste not; handle not" he says that they are "after the
commandments and doctrines of men" (2:21–22).

That last phrase is Isaiah's. J. B. Lightfoot notes that "The expression is
taken ultimately from Isaiah xxix. 13", the verse Jesus quotes against the
elders in Mark 7, and that the coincidences between Paul's language and Jesus'
words in Matthew 15 and Mark 7 "are striking, and suggest that the Apostle had
this discourse in his mind". So the relation is recorded as an allusion, on
Lightfoot's authority, and not as a quotation: Paul gives no "as it is written"
(`colossiansAlludesToIsaiah`, `colossiansAlludesToMark7`).

### What these texts deliver

Together they deliver the principle Mark 7 delivers: God's word judges human
tradition, and no commandment of men may be taught as God's word
(`jesusAndPaulPrinciple_establishes`). The step from the texts to the principle
is rated `wellSupported`, as Mark 7's is. Thomas Aquinas, lecturing on Galatians,
grants the text and the principle with it: "nothing is to be taught except what
is contained, either implicitly or explicitly, in the Gospels and epistles and
Sacred Scripture". What he denies is Calvin's reading of "any other gospel" as
any gospel "to which the inventions of other men are added". For Aquinas Paul's
"besides" means "adding something completely alien". That is a dispute about how
far the principle reaches, not about the principle.

### What they do not deliver

They do not deliver sola scriptura. Add them to Mark 7 and to the step from the
principle to the sole rule, leave out the one premise Rome denies — that no
unwritten tradition can now be shown to be apostolic — and the sole rule is
still open: neither it nor its denial follows
(`every_text_without_the_hinge_leaves_the_sole_rule_open`). Nor do they reach
Trent read as the apostolic word handed on unwritten, which can be held with
every one of them (`jesus_and_paul_do_not_reach_the_apostolic_word`). Rome
answers that Paul also tells the Corinthians to "keep the ordinances, as I
delivered them to you" (1 Corinthians 11:2), so that his measure is where a
teaching came from, not whether it was written down.

So the texts show that the principle does not hang on one story in the Gospels,
and they leave the Reformation's question where Mark 7 left it. In the dispute
over Mark 7 the principle already prevails, and the least-supported link in its
case is rated `wellSupported`, the second of the four ratings. A second route
rated the same would not change that, so these texts join the Protestant
position (`protestant`) and not the dispute.

#### Paul and Isaiah 29:13

<a id="colossians2_22"></a>
**`colossians2_22`**

Colossians 2:22 — "after the commandments and doctrines of men".

```lean
def colossians2_22 : Passage :=
  { book := Book.colossians, chapter := 2, verse := 22 }
```

<a id="colossiansAlludesToIsaiah"></a>
**`colossiansAlludesToIsaiah`**

**Colossians 2:22 alludes to Isaiah 29:13.** Typed `.allusion`, not
`.quotation`: Paul introduces no citation, and Lightfoot says only that "The
expression is taken ultimately from Isaiah xxix. 13" (p. 204). Rated
`plausible`: only Lightfoot is cited for it, and no reader who denies it has
been looked for.

```lean
def colossiansAlludesToIsaiah : IntertextEdge :=
  { fromPassage := colossians2_22,
    toPassage := Scripture.isaiah29_13, relation := RelationType.allusion,
    source :=
      { primary := Reference.work lightfootColossians (Bib.Locus.page 204),
        tradition := Tradition.christianHistoricalGrammatical,
        confidence := Confidence.plausible } }
```

<a id="colossiansAlludesToMark7"></a>
**`colossiansAlludesToMark7`**

**Colossians 2:22 alludes to Jesus' words in Mark 7.** Lightfoot finds the
coincidences with "our Lord's words as related in the Gospels (Matt. xv. 1—20,
Mark vii. 1—23)" "striking", and judges that they "suggest that the Apostle had
this discourse in his mind" (p. 204): both argue from the perishing of food, and
both connect such rules with Isaiah's denunciation. An allusion, and rated
`plausible`, for the same reasons as `colossiansAlludesToIsaiah`.

```lean
def colossiansAlludesToMark7 : IntertextEdge :=
  { fromPassage := colossians2_22, toPassage := Scripture.mark7_7,
    relation := RelationType.allusion,
    source :=
      { primary := Reference.work lightfootColossians (Bib.Locus.page 204),
        tradition := Tradition.christianHistoricalGrammatical,
        confidence := Confidence.plausible } }
```

#### The principle, from Jesus and Paul

<a id="jesusAndPaulPrinciple"></a>
**`jesusAndPaulPrinciple`** — Jesus and Paul (God's word judges human tradition)

**The principle from Jesus' sayings and Paul's letters**: John 10:35,
Matthew 5:18, Galatians 1:8–9 and Colossians 2:8, 20–22, and the step from them
to the principle that God's word judges human tradition. It claims nothing
about Scripture's place among the rules of faith.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{#claim-40}{P_{40}}\\) — John 10:35 — the scripture cannot be broken
- (2) \\(\href{#claim-41}{P_{41}}\\) — Matthew 5:18 — one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law, till all be fulfilled
- (3) \\(\href{#claim-42}{P_{42}}\\) — Galatians 1:8–9 — though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel than that which we have preached, let him be accursed
- (4) \\(\href{#claim-43}{P_{43}}\\) — Colossians 2:8, 20–22 — after the tradition of men, and not after Christ; after the commandments and doctrines of men
- (5) \\((\href{#claim-40}{P_{40}} \land \href{#claim-41}{P_{41}} \land \href{#claim-42}{P_{42}} \land \href{#claim-43}{P_{43}}) \rightarrow \href{#claim-37}{P_{37}}\\)
- \\(\vdash\\) \\(\href{#claim-37}{P_{37}}\\) — *at issue:* God's word judges human tradition: no commandment of men may be taught as God's word, and a tradition that voids God's command is void

</div>

No premise here rests on scripture alone.

<a id="everyTextWithoutTheHinge"></a>
**`everyTextWithoutTheHinge`**

Every text the argument draws the principle from, Mark 7's and the others,
with the step from the principle to the sole rule, and without the premise that
no unwritten tradition can now be shown to be apostolic.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{#claim-3}{P_{3}}\\) — Mark 7:1–13 (Matthew 15:1–9) — Jesus rebukes the elders' tradition, Corban above all, for voiding God's command
- (2) \\(\href{#claim-40}{P_{40}}\\) — John 10:35 — the scripture cannot be broken
- (3) \\(\href{#claim-41}{P_{41}}\\) — Matthew 5:18 — one jot or one tittle shall in no wise pass from the law, till all be fulfilled
- (4) \\(\href{#claim-42}{P_{42}}\\) — Galatians 1:8–9 — though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel than that which we have preached, let him be accursed
- (5) \\(\href{#claim-43}{P_{43}}\\) — Colossians 2:8, 20–22 — after the tradition of men, and not after Christ; after the commandments and doctrines of men
- (6) \\(\href{#claim-3}{P_{3}} \rightarrow \href{#claim-37}{P_{37}}\\) — *would give:* God's word judges human tradition: no commandment of men may be taught as God's word, and a tradition that voids God's command is void
- (7) \\((\href{#claim-40}{P_{40}} \land \href{#claim-41}{P_{41}} \land \href{#claim-42}{P_{42}} \land \href{#claim-43}{P_{43}}) \rightarrow \href{#claim-37}{P_{37}}\\) — *would give:* God's word judges human tradition: no commandment of men may be taught as God's word, and a tradition that voids God's command is void
- (8) \\((\href{#claim-37}{P_{37}} \land \href{#claim-39}{P_{39}}) \rightarrow \href{#claim-9}{P_{9}}\\) — *would give:* Scripture is the sole infallible rule of faith

</div>

<a id="jesusAndPaulPrinciple_establishes"></a>
**`jesusAndPaulPrinciple_establishes`**

**Jesus and Paul deliver the principle without Mark 7.** God's word judges
human tradition, from four texts and the step from them, rated `wellSupported`:
Aquinas grants Galatians 1:8 and the principle, and denies only that every
addition to the gospel is "another gospel".

What this does not claim: that the principle makes Scripture the only measure of
tradition. Aquinas and Rome grant the principle and deny that.

```lean
theorem jesusAndPaulPrinciple_establishes : Establishes jesusAndPaulPrinciple
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="jesusAndPaulPrinciple_is_satisfiable"></a>
**`jesusAndPaulPrinciple_is_satisfiable`**

The principle from Jesus and Paul can be held without contradiction: the
Reformed reading.

```lean
theorem jesusAndPaulPrinciple_is_satisfiable : Satisfiable
    jesusAndPaulPrinciple.premises
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="jesus_and_paul_do_not_reach_the_apostolic_word"></a>
**`jesus_and_paul_do_not_reach_the_apostolic_word`**

**Jesus and Paul do not reach Trent read as the apostolic word.** Trent,
read as receiving the apostolic word handed on unwritten, can be held with every
premise of the principle from Jesus and Paul: Rome's reading, on which God's
word judges human tradition and some unwritten tradition is the apostles' own,
known to be so. The same holds of Mark 7
(`mark7_does_not_reach_the_apostolic_word`).

```lean
theorem jesus_and_paul_do_not_reach_the_apostolic_word : Satisfiable
    (jesusAndPaulPrinciple.premises ++ tridentineAsApostolicWord.premises)
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="every_text_without_the_hinge_leaves_the_sole_rule_open"></a>
**`every_text_without_the_hinge_leaves_the_sole_rule_open`**

**Every text, without the premise Rome denies, leaves the sole rule open.**
Grant Mark 7, John 10:35, Matthew 5:18, Galatians 1:8–9 and Colossians 2, the
principle they deliver, and the step from the principle to the sole rule; leave
out only the premise that no unwritten tradition can now be shown to be
apostolic. Sola scriptura neither follows nor fails. Rome's reading grants all of
it and denies the sole rule; the Reformed reading grants all of it and holds the
sole rule. One fact, as with Mark 7 alone
(`mark7_without_the_hinge_leaves_the_sole_rule_open`): more texts for the
principle do not supply the premise the step to the sole rule needs.

```lean
theorem every_text_without_the_hinge_leaves_the_sole_rule_open : Independent
    everyTextWithoutTheHinge (p Claim.scriptureIsSoleInfallibleRule)
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

## TestimonyArguments.SolaScriptura.Acts15 — the council at Jerusalem, read both ways

Acts 15 tells of the council at Jerusalem, and both sides of the Reformation
read it as their own. It begins with a demand: "certain men which
came down from Judaea taught the brethren, and said, Except ye be circumcised
after the manner of Moses, ye cannot be saved" (15:1). The apostles and elders
meet. Peter asks "why tempt ye God, to put a yoke upon the neck of the
disciples, which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear? But we believe
that through the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ we shall be saved, even as they"
(15:10–11). James answers from the prophets: "to this agree the words of the
prophets; as it is written, After this I will return, and will build again the
tabernacle of David, which is fallen down" (15:15–16, quoting Amos 9:11–12).
The council writes to the gentile churches, "For it seemed good to the Holy
Ghost, and to us, to lay upon you no greater burden than these necessary things"
(15:28), and Paul and Silas, going through the cities, "delivered them the
decrees for to keep, that were ordained of the apostles and elders which were at
Jerusalem" (16:4).

James's words are a quotation, not an allusion: he introduces them "as it is
written" (`acts15QuotesAmos`). Calvin notes that the place "is not cited word
for word as it is in the prophet". Luke gives Amos close to the Greek
translation, the Septuagint. Where the Hebrew of Amos 9:12 reads "That they may
possess the remnant of Edom", the Septuagint reads "that the remnant of men may
seek" (ὅπως ἐκζητήσωσιν οἱ κατάλοιποι τῶν ἀνθρώπων), and so does Acts: "That the
residue of men might seek after the Lord".

### The Reformed reading

The custom of Moses was the oldest tradition Israel had, and God had given it.
The council did not let even that be laid on the gentiles as a condition of
salvation: Peter answered it with the gospel and James with Scripture. So the
gospel judged even the oldest tradition, and the council judged by Scripture.
Calvin says of 15:15 that the apostles "took nothing to themselves imperiously,
but did reverently follow that which was prescribed in the word of God", and
were not ashamed "to profess themselves to be the scholars of the Scripture".
The Westminster Confession draws the rule for councils after them: their
decrees bind "if consonant to the Word of God", and "All synods or councils since
the apostles' times, whether general or particular, may err, and many have
erred; therefore they are not to be made the rule of faith or practice, but to
be used as a help in both" (XXXI.3–4, in the numbering of 1647). The Protestant
position reads Acts 15 this way (`acts15ReformedLine`).

### Rome's reading

The council's letter claims more than agreement with Scripture: "it seemed good
to the Holy Ghost, and to us". Joseph Wilhelm, writing on general councils in
the *Catholic Encyclopedia* of 1908, takes it as "the mind of the Apostles":
they "put the seal of supreme authority on their decisions in attributing them
to the joint action of the Spirit of God and of themselves", and general
councils in union with the pope have the same "infallible authority". The
decrees were then handed on to the churches to keep: "delivered" in 16:4
(παρεδίδοσαν) is the verb whose noun is "tradition" (παράδοσις). Tradition III,
the position resting on Vatican I, reads Acts 15 this way (`acts15RomanLine`).

### Where the readings part: the apostles' office

The council at Jerusalem had apostles in it, and a council after them has none.
So both readings pass through a second question: did the apostles' own office
end with them, or does it continue in those who succeed them?

The Reformers say it ended. The apostle chosen in Judas's place had to be one of
the men "which have companied with us all the time that the Lord Jesus went in
and out among us", to be "a witness with us of his resurrection" (Acts 1:21–22).
Paul counts himself the last such witness: "last of all he was seen of me also,
as of one born out of due time" (1 Corinthians 15:8). Peter puts Paul's letters
with "the other scriptures" (2 Peter 3:15–16), and Paul writes as "an apostle of
Jesus Christ" beside "Timothy our brother" (2 Corinthians 1:1; Colossians 1:1).
Calvin draws the conclusion in the *Institutes*: the offices of apostle,
prophet and evangelist "were not instituted in the Church to be perpetual", and
the twelve, "to the number of whom Paul was afterwards added", were
"distinguished from others by a peculiar title" (IV.iii.4–5). He does not say
that nothing passes on. Pastors "have the same function as apostles", the
preaching of the gospel and the sacraments, but not their office
(`apostlesOfficeEndedLine`).

Rome says it continues. The council was not the apostles alone but "the
apostles and elders" (15:6, 22–23; 16:4). Peter applies the Psalm to Judas, "his
bishoprick (ἐπισκοπή) let another take" (Acts 1:20); Paul bids Timothy "commit thou
to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also" (2 Timothy 2:2); and
Clement of Rome, writing to Corinth near the end of the first century, records
that the apostles appointed bishops and deacons and "afterwards gave
instructions, that when these should fall asleep, other approved men should
succeed them in their ministry" (1 Clement 44). The Second Vatican Council
concludes that "the apostles' office of nurturing the Church is permanent, and
is to be exercised without interruption by the sacred order of bishops"
(*Lumen Gentium* 20) (`apostolicSuccessionLine`). Calvin grants Acts 1:20, that
"another may succeed him", and answers at Acts 1:21 that the apostleship "is not
without the preaching of the gospel", so that the bishops of his day "brag that
they are the successors of the apostles; but wherein are they like unto them?"

One text cuts across the Reformed reading of the salutations. 1 Thessalonians is
from "Paul, and Silvanus, and Timotheus" (1:1), and says "we might have been
burdensome, as the apostles of Christ" (2:6). If "apostles" takes in Silvanus
and Timothy, the title was wider than the eyewitnesses. Calvin reads it of Paul
alone, "inasmuch as he was an Apostle of Christ", and H. Coppieters, in the
*Catholic Encyclopedia*, lists the verse among the passages "in which the
extension of the word Apostle is doubtful". The verse is recorded for what it
says and is a ground of neither line, because no reader cited here builds on it
either way.

Each step about the office is rated `disputed`. *Lumen Gentium* grants the texts
of the first and denies its conclusion; Calvin grants those of the second and
denies its conclusion. So the texts alone leave the question open
(`apostolic_texts_leave_the_office_open`). Whether the decree's four abstentions
(15:20, 29) apply the laws Leviticus 17–18 gives for the stranger, so that the
council applied Moses rather than making new law, is not encoded: no
commentator who argues it has been read for this library.

### What the texts settle, and what they do not

Each reading grants every text the other reads. The Westminster Confession
cites Acts 15:27–31 and 16:4 as its own proof that a council's decrees bind, and
Wilhelm, as a Catholic, grants Peter's and James's words. What they part over
is the step from the texts to councils after the apostles, which passes through
the apostles' office, and each step is rated `disputed` because the other side's
reader grants its texts and denies its conclusion.

So the two readings cannot be held together
(`acts15_readings_cannot_be_held_together`), and the texts by themselves do not
choose between them: grant all seven texts, without any step, and whether a
council binds with the Spirit's authority neither follows nor fails
(`acts15_texts_leave_the_council_open`).

Nor does Rome's reading reach the premise the Mark 7 case for sola scriptura
needs, that no unwritten tradition can now be shown to be apostolic. The
decrees handed on in 16:4 were not unwritten: "they wrote letters by them"
(15:23), and the letter is in Scripture (15:23–29). Grant Rome's reading of Acts
15 and that the decree was written, and the premise about unwritten tradition is
left exactly where it was (`romes_reading_of_acts15_leaves_unwritten_tradition_open`).

These lines join the Protestant and Vatican I positions, and not the dispute
over Mark 7. That dispute is about tradition, and none of its parties says
anything about councils, so neither reading of Acts 15 would meet a party
there.
