#### Readings, written down

<a id="reformedOnTheCouncilReading"></a>
**`reformedOnTheCouncilReading`**

The Reformed world, on Acts 15: every text holds, no commandment of men is
bound as God's word, the apostles' own office ended with them, and a council
after the apostles may err.

```lean
def reformedOnTheCouncilReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.mensCommandmentBindsAsGodsWord => False
    | Claim.councilBindsWithTheSpiritsAuthority => False
    | x => True
```

<a id="successionHoldsReading"></a>
**`successionHoldsReading`**

A world in which every claim of the argument holds but one, that the
apostles' own office ended with them. It is no one's position; it shows that
Rome's reading of Acts 15 can be held with the premise about unwritten
tradition.

```lean
def successionHoldsReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.apostlesOfficeEndedWithThem => False
    | x => True
```

#### What follows

<a id="acts15Reformed_establishes"></a>
**`acts15Reformed_establishes`**

**The Reformed reading of Acts 15 holds, given its steps.** From 15:1,
15:10–11 and 15:15–17, and from the apostles' office having ended with them, a
council after the apostles does not bind with the Spirit's own authority: it
binds as far as it agrees with Scripture. Both steps are rated `disputed`:
Wilhelm grants the texts of Acts 15 and denies the conclusion, and *Lumen
Gentium* 20 grants the texts on the apostles and denies that their office
ended.

What this does not claim: that councils have no authority. The Westminster
Confession, which holds this reading, says their decrees are "to be received with
reverence and submission" when they agree with the word.

```lean
theorem acts15Reformed_establishes : Establishes acts15Reformed
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="acts15Reformed_is_satisfiable"></a>
**`acts15Reformed_is_satisfiable`**

The Reformed reading of Acts 15 can be held without contradiction.

```lean
theorem acts15Reformed_is_satisfiable : Satisfiable acts15Reformed.premises
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="acts15Roman_establishes"></a>
**`acts15Roman_establishes`**

**Rome's reading of Acts 15 holds, given its steps.** From 15:28 and 16:4,
the council of "the apostles and elders", and the apostles' office continuing in
their successors, a general council binds with the Holy Spirit's authority. Both
steps are rated `disputed`: the Westminster Confession grants the texts of Acts
15 and denies the conclusion, and Calvin grants the succession texts and denies
that the apostles' office continues.

```lean
theorem acts15Roman_establishes : Establishes acts15Roman
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="acts15Roman_is_satisfiable"></a>
**`acts15Roman_is_satisfiable`**

Rome's reading of Acts 15 can be held without contradiction: Rome's world, in
which God's word judges human tradition, some unwritten tradition is known to be
apostolic, the apostles' office continues in their successors, and a general
council binds with the Spirit's authority.

```lean
theorem acts15Roman_is_satisfiable : Satisfiable acts15Roman.premises
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="acts15_readings_cannot_be_held_together"></a>
**`acts15_readings_cannot_be_held_together`**

**The two readings of Acts 15 cannot be held together.** One concludes that a
council after the apostles may err, the other that a general council binds with
the Spirit's authority and cannot. They also part on the way there, over whether
the apostles' office ended with them. Since every text either reads is granted
by both, what they part over is the four steps, each rated `disputed`.

What this does not claim: that either reading is wrong. It shows only that a
reader must choose between them.

```lean
theorem acts15_readings_cannot_be_held_together : ¬Satisfiable
    (acts15Reformed.premises ++ acts15Roman.premises)
-- axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound
```

<a id="acts15_texts_leave_the_council_open"></a>
**`acts15_texts_leave_the_council_open`**

**The texts of Acts 15 do not settle the council's authority.** Grant
15:1, 15:6, 15:10–11, 15:15–17, 15:22–29 and 15:28, and 16:4, without either
reading's step: whether a general council binds with the Spirit's authority
neither follows nor fails. The Reformed reading grants every text and denies it; Rome's
grants every text and holds it. One fact, not two: the texts alone establish
neither reading and block neither.

```lean
theorem acts15_texts_leave_the_council_open : Independent acts15Texts (p
    Claim.councilBindsWithTheSpiritsAuthority)
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="romes_reading_of_acts15_leaves_unwritten_tradition_open"></a>
**`romes_reading_of_acts15_leaves_unwritten_tradition_open`**

**Rome's reading of Acts 15 does not reach unwritten tradition.** Grant that
"it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us", that the decrees were delivered
to keep, that the council was "the apostles and elders", the texts on the
apostles' successors, Rome's steps from them, and that the decree went out as a
letter (15:23–29): whether any unwritten tradition can now be shown to be
apostolic neither follows nor fails. Rome's world grants all of it and denies
the premise; a world in which every claim of the argument holds but one, that
the apostles' office ended with them, grants all of it and holds the premise.
What the council handed on was written, so it is no instance of the unwritten
tradition the Mark 7 case turns on.

```lean
theorem romes_reading_of_acts15_leaves_unwritten_tradition_open : Independent
    (acts15Roman.premises ++ [p Claim.acts15_23_29DecreeWritten]) (p
    Claim.noUnwrittenTraditionShownApostolic)
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

#### The apostles' office

<a id="apostlesOfficeEnded_establishes"></a>
**`apostlesOfficeEnded_establishes`**

**The apostles' office ended, given Calvin's step.** From Acts 1:21–22, 1
Corinthians 15:8, 2 Peter 3:15–16 and Paul's salutations, the apostles' own
office ended with them. The step is rated `disputed`: *Lumen Gentium* 20 grants
the texts and holds that the office is permanent in the bishops.

What this does not claim: that nothing of the apostles' work passes on. Calvin,
who holds it, says pastors "have the same function as apostles".

```lean
theorem apostlesOfficeEnded_establishes : Establishes apostlesOfficeEnded
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="apostlesOfficeEnded_is_satisfiable"></a>
**`apostlesOfficeEnded_is_satisfiable`**

That the apostles' office ended can be held without contradiction.

```lean
theorem apostlesOfficeEnded_is_satisfiable : Satisfiable
    apostlesOfficeEnded.premises
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="apostolicSuccession_establishes"></a>
**`apostolicSuccession_establishes`**

**The apostles' office continues, given Rome's step.** From Acts 1:20, 2
Timothy 2:2 and 1 Clement 42 and 44, the apostles' office did not end with them.
The step is rated `disputed`: Calvin grants the texts and holds that the office
was not "instituted in the Church to be perpetual".

```lean
theorem apostolicSuccession_establishes : Establishes apostolicSuccession
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="apostolicSuccession_is_satisfiable"></a>
**`apostolicSuccession_is_satisfiable`**

That the apostles' office continues can be held without contradiction.

```lean
theorem apostolicSuccession_is_satisfiable : Satisfiable
    apostolicSuccession.premises
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="apostolic_texts_leave_the_office_open"></a>
**`apostolic_texts_leave_the_office_open`**

**The texts on the apostles do not settle whether their office ended.** Grant
Acts 1:20 and 1:21–22, 1 Corinthians 15:8, 2 Peter 3:15–16, Paul's salutations,
2 Timothy 2:2, what 1 Clement 42 and 44 records, 1 Thessalonians 2:6, and the
council of "the apostles and elders", without either side's step: whether the
apostles' own office ended with them neither follows nor fails. Rome's world
grants every text and denies it; the Reformed world grants every text and holds
it. One fact, not two: the texts establish neither reading and block
neither.

```lean
theorem apostolic_texts_leave_the_office_open : Independent apostolicTexts (p
    Claim.apostlesOfficeEndedWithThem)
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

## TestimonyArguments.SolaScriptura.MosesSeat — Moses' seat, read both ways

A reader who has followed Jesus against the elders in Mark 7 meets him, a few
days before his death, saying something that sounds like the opposite. "The
scribes and the Pharisees sit in Moses' seat: All therefore whatsoever they bid
you observe, that observe and do; but do not ye after their works: for they
say, and do not" (Matthew 23:2–3). The "seat" (καθέδρα) is a teacher's chair.
The verb for "observe" (τηρεῖτε) is the one Mark 7:9 uses for keeping "your own
tradition", in the text the SBL Greek New Testament prints; the Nestle-Aland
edition prints "establish" (στήσητε) there instead. J. W. Wenham, in his 1953
lecture on Jesus and the Old Testament, finds the saying "even more remarkable"
than Matthew 5:17–20, and comments: "To Jesus scribal lore was valuable if
linked with spiritual understanding". Jesus upholds the teaching of men he goes on to
rebuke. Both sides of the Reformation read the saying, and they read it in
opposite directions.

### The Reformed reading

The same discourse condemns a teaching of the same scribes: "Woe unto you, ye
blind guides, which say, Whosoever shall swear by the temple, it is nothing; but
whosoever shall swear by the gold of the temple, he is a debtor!" (23:16–22). So
Jesus cannot be binding his hearers to everything the scribes say. Calvin takes
"Moses' seat" to mean the law taught from it: "to sit in the chair of Moses is
nothing else than to teach, according to the Law of God, how we ought to live",
and so "Christ exhorts the people to obey the scribes, only so far as they
adhere to the pure and simple exposition of the Law". He grants that the seat
"denotes, at the same time, a lawful calling", and that the scribes were to be
heard "because they were the public teachers of the Church". What he denies is
that the station is enough. "The Papists reckon it enough, that those who issue
laws should possess the title and occupy the station". Were that so, there would
be "no good ground" for Jesus' saying in Matthew 15:9, the parallel of Mark 7,
"that it is in vain to worship God by the commandments of men". On this reading
an office in the Church is heard as far as it teaches God's word, and not for
its seat alone. The Protestant position reads Matthew 23 this way
(`mosesSeatReformedLine`).

### Rome's reading

Cornelius a Lapide, the Jesuit commentator of the early seventeenth century,
reads the seat as "the honour, dignity, and authority of teaching and
commanding, which Moses had with the Jews, and to which the Scribes had
succeeded", and draws the Church's case from it: "In like manner, the chair of
S. Peter is used to signify the power and authority of teaching and ruling all
the faithful throughout the world, in which the Roman Pontiffs succeed S.
Peter". Jesus' "all things" means "all things not contrary to Moses and the
Law": the corban teaching of Mark 7 "was contrary to the Law, as Christ showed",
and was not to be followed. In everything else the scribes were to be obeyed,
even in dogmas "vain and foolish, and therefore not binding", which could "yet
serve for the merit of blind and simple obedience, and for reverence of the
sacerdotal order". And "Christians ought to bear in mind these words of Christ
when they see certain Bishops, Pastors, and Magistrates not living in accordance
with the law of Christ". On this reading those who hold the Church's teaching
office are heeded for the seat they hold, in whatever is not contrary to God's
law, even when they live ill. Tradition III, the position resting on Vatican I,
reads Matthew 23 this way (`mosesSeatRomanLine`).

The claim is one of authority, not of infallibility, which is the power of a
teaching that cannot err. Lapide goes on to say that the pope "cannot err" when
he defines the faith, but Moses' seat cannot carry that: the scribes who sat in
it taught things "contrary to the Law". The library does not draw it from this
text.

### What the texts settle, and what they do not

The two readers grant each other's texts. Lapide calls the scribes of 23:16
"rightly called by Christ blind guides", and grants that Jesus condemned the
corban teaching; Calvin grants that Jesus commands the scribes to be heard. What
they part over is the measure. For Calvin an office binds as far as it teaches
the law, and for Lapide in everything not contrary to it. So each reading's step
is rated `disputed`, a rating given when a cited reader grants a step's texts
and denies its conclusion. The two readings cannot be held together
(`moses_seat_readings_cannot_be_held_together`). Grant Mark 7, the principle it
delivers that God's word judges human tradition, and Matthew 23:2–3 and
23:16–22, without either step: whether the teaching office is heeded for its
seat neither follows nor fails (`mark7_and_moses_seat_leave_the_office_open`).
So each reading holds Jesus' two sayings together, in its own way, and the
texts alone do not choose between them.

Nor does Rome's reading undo the case for sola scriptura from Mark 7. That case
concludes that Scripture is the sole infallible rule, and Rome's reading of
Moses' seat is about authority, not infallibility. A reader can grant both
(`romes_reading_of_moses_seat_can_be_held_with_mark7s_case`).

These lines join the Protestant and Vatican I positions, and not the dispute
over Mark 7. None of the parties to that dispute says anything about the
teaching office, so neither reading of Matthew 23 would meet a party there.

#### The two readings

<a id="mosesSeatReformed"></a>
**`mosesSeatReformed`** — Moses' seat, the Reformed reading (heard as far as it teaches the word)

**Moses' seat, the Reformed reading**: Matthew 23:2–3, the "blind guides" of
23:16–22 and Mark 7, and the step from them to the teaching office: an office in
the Church is heard as far as it teaches God's word, and not for its seat
alone.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{#claim-51}{P_{51}}\\) — Matthew 23:2–3 — the scribes and the Pharisees sit in Moses' seat: all whatsoever they bid you observe, that observe and do; but do not ye after their works
- (2) \\(\href{#claim-52}{P_{52}}\\) — Matthew 23:16–22 — woe unto you, ye blind guides, which say, Whosoever shall swear by the temple, it is nothing
- (3) \\(\href{#claim-3}{P_{3}}\\) — Mark 7:1–13 (Matthew 15:1–9) — Jesus rebukes the elders' tradition, Corban above all, for voiding God's command
- (4) \\((\href{#claim-51}{P_{51}} \land \href{#claim-52}{P_{52}} \land \href{#claim-3}{P_{3}}) \rightarrow \lnot \href{#claim-53}{P_{53}}\\)
- \\(\vdash\\) \\(\lnot \href{#claim-53}{P_{53}}\\) — *at issue, the denial of:* Those who hold the Church's teaching office are to be heeded for the seat they hold, in whatever is not contrary to God's law, even when they live ill

</div>

Grounded in scripture alone: Matthew 23:16–22 — woe unto you, ye blind guides, which say, Whosoever shall swear by the temple, it is nothing.

<a id="mosesSeatRoman"></a>
**`mosesSeatRoman`** — Moses' seat, Rome's reading (the office heeded for its seat)

**Moses' seat, Rome's reading**: Matthew 23:2–3, and the step from it to the
teaching office: those who hold it are heeded for the seat they hold, in
whatever is not contrary to God's law.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{#claim-51}{P_{51}}\\) — Matthew 23:2–3 — the scribes and the Pharisees sit in Moses' seat: all whatsoever they bid you observe, that observe and do; but do not ye after their works
- (2) \\(\href{#claim-51}{P_{51}} \rightarrow \href{#claim-53}{P_{53}}\\)
- \\(\vdash\\) \\(\href{#claim-53}{P_{53}}\\) — *at issue:* Those who hold the Church's teaching office are to be heeded for the seat they hold, in whatever is not contrary to God's law, even when they live ill

</div>

No premise here rests on scripture alone.

<a id="mosesSeatTexts"></a>
**`mosesSeatTexts`**

Mark 7 and the principle it delivers, with every text either reading of
Moses' seat reads: Matthew 23:2–3 and 23:16–22. No step from Matthew 23.

<div class="testimony-derivation">

- (1) \\(\href{#claim-3}{P_{3}}\\) — Mark 7:1–13 (Matthew 15:1–9) — Jesus rebukes the elders' tradition, Corban above all, for voiding God's command
- (2) \\(\href{#claim-3}{P_{3}} \rightarrow \href{#claim-37}{P_{37}}\\) — *would give:* God's word judges human tradition: no commandment of men may be taught as God's word, and a tradition that voids God's command is void
- (3) \\(\href{#claim-37}{P_{37}} \rightarrow \lnot \href{#claim-38}{P_{38}}\\) — *would deny:* A commandment of men may rightly be bound on the Church as God's word
- (4) \\(\href{#claim-51}{P_{51}}\\) — Matthew 23:2–3 — the scribes and the Pharisees sit in Moses' seat: all whatsoever they bid you observe, that observe and do; but do not ye after their works
- (5) \\(\href{#claim-52}{P_{52}}\\) — Matthew 23:16–22 — woe unto you, ye blind guides, which say, Whosoever shall swear by the temple, it is nothing

</div>

#### Readings, written down

<a id="reformedOnTheSeatReading"></a>
**`reformedOnTheSeatReading`**

The Reformed world, on Moses' seat: every text holds, no commandment of men
is bound as God's word, and those who hold the teaching office are heard as far
as they teach God's word, not for their seat alone.

```lean
def reformedOnTheSeatReading : Valuation Claim :=
  fun a =>
    match a with
    | Claim.mensCommandmentBindsAsGodsWord => False
    | Claim.teachingOfficeHeardByItsSeat => False
    | x => True
```

#### What follows

<a id="mosesSeatReformed_establishes"></a>
**`mosesSeatReformed_establishes`**

**The Reformed reading of Moses' seat holds, given its step.** From Matthew
23:2–3, 23:16–22 and Mark 7, the teaching office in the Church is heard as far as
it teaches God's word, and not for its seat alone. The step is rated `disputed`:
Cornelius a Lapide grants the texts and holds that the scribes were to be obeyed
in "all things not contrary to Moses and the Law".

What this does not claim: that the office has no authority. Calvin, who holds
this reading, says Christ "commands that the scribes should be heard, because
they were the public teachers of the Church".

```lean
theorem mosesSeatReformed_establishes : Establishes mosesSeatReformed
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="mosesSeatReformed_is_satisfiable"></a>
**`mosesSeatReformed_is_satisfiable`**

The Reformed reading of Moses' seat can be held without contradiction.

```lean
theorem mosesSeatReformed_is_satisfiable : Satisfiable
    mosesSeatReformed.premises
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="mosesSeatRoman_establishes"></a>
**`mosesSeatRoman_establishes`**

**Rome's reading of Moses' seat holds, given its step.** From Matthew
23:2–3, those who hold the Church's teaching office are heeded for the seat they
hold, in whatever is not contrary to God's law, even when they live ill. The step
is rated `disputed`: Calvin grants the text and holds that the scribes were to be
obeyed "only so far as they adhere to the pure and simple exposition of the
Law".

What this does not claim: that the office cannot err. Its own reader, Lapide,
says the scribes in Moses' seat taught things "contrary to the Law".

```lean
theorem mosesSeatRoman_establishes : Establishes mosesSeatRoman
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="mosesSeatRoman_is_satisfiable"></a>
**`mosesSeatRoman_is_satisfiable`**

Rome's reading of Moses' seat can be held without contradiction: Rome's
world, in which God's word judges human tradition, some unwritten tradition is
known to be apostolic, and every other claim of the argument holds, among them
that the teaching office is heeded for its seat.

```lean
theorem mosesSeatRoman_is_satisfiable : Satisfiable mosesSeatRoman.premises
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="moses_seat_readings_cannot_be_held_together"></a>
**`moses_seat_readings_cannot_be_held_together`**

**The two readings of Moses' seat cannot be held together.** One concludes
that the teaching office is heard only as far as it teaches God's word, the
other that it is heeded for its seat in whatever is not contrary to that word.
Both grant Matthew 23:2–3, so what they part over is the two steps, each rated
`disputed`.

What this does not claim: that either reading is wrong. It shows only that a
reader must choose between them.

```lean
theorem moses_seat_readings_cannot_be_held_together : ¬Satisfiable
    (mosesSeatReformed.premises ++ mosesSeatRoman.premises)
-- axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound
```

<a id="mark7_and_moses_seat_leave_the_office_open"></a>
**`mark7_and_moses_seat_leave_the_office_open`**

**Mark 7 and Moses' seat leave the teaching office open.** Grant Mark 7, the
principle it delivers that God's word judges human tradition, and Matthew 23:2–3
and 23:16–22, without either reading's step from Matthew 23: whether the teaching
office is heeded for its seat neither follows nor fails. The Reformed reading
grants every text and the principle, and denies it; Rome's grants them all and
holds it. So each reading holds Jesus' two sayings together, and the texts by
themselves choose neither. One fact, not two: the texts establish neither
reading and block neither.

```lean
theorem mark7_and_moses_seat_leave_the_office_open : Independent
    mosesSeatTexts (p Claim.teachingOfficeHeardByItsSeat)
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

<a id="romes_reading_of_moses_seat_can_be_held_with_mark7s_case"></a>
**`romes_reading_of_moses_seat_can_be_held_with_mark7s_case`**

**Rome's reading of Moses' seat can be held with Mark 7's case for sola
scriptura.** Grant Mark 7, its principle, the premise that no unwritten tradition
can now be shown to be apostolic, and the step to the sole rule, and with them
Rome's reading of Matthew 23:2–3: nothing contradicts. The witness is a world in
which every claim of the argument holds but one, that a commandment of men may
be bound as God's word. Rome's reading claims that the teaching office is to be
heeded, not that it cannot err, so it leaves Scripture the sole infallible rule.

What this does not claim: that the Reformers accept Rome's reading. Calvin
denies it; the Protestant position holds the Reformed reading instead.

```lean
theorem romes_reading_of_moses_seat_can_be_held_with_mark7s_case : Satisfiable
    (mark7Case.premises ++ mosesSeatRoman.premises)
-- axioms: propext, Quot.sound
```

## TestimonyArguments.SolaScriptura.Dispute — what Mark 7 decides between Rome and the Reformers

`Mark7.lean` asks what each position entails. This module asks what happens when
they meet. Five parties: Mark 7's principle; Mark 7's case for sola scriptura;
Trent, as it states its position; and Trent with its tradition read each of the
two ways the dilemma `whatTrentsTraditionIs` names. Who defeats whom is not
stipulated — each defeat, and each absence of one, is computed from the parties'
premises and checked by the kernel (see `Testimony.Logic.Dispute`).

### How to read the verdicts

- **Defeats.** One position contradicts another — denies one of its premises,
  its conclusion, or a claim it derives on the way — and is not the weaker of
  the two. A defeat that runs both ways is a *standoff*.
- **Weakest link.** A position is only as strong as its least-supported premise
  or step. Ratings run from `disputed`, the lowest, through `plausible` and
  `wellSupported`, to `consensus`.
- **Forced.** Accepted however every standoff is resolved: nothing attacks it
  that it cannot rule out.
- **Can be defended.** Held by some consistent position that answers every
  attack on its members, itself or through an ally.
- **Not forced.** Some consistent position leaves it out. Not forced is not
  false: the dispute, as argued, cannot make a reader accept it.
- **Cannot be defended.** No consistent position can hold it and answer its
  attackers.
- **A defensible position that cannot be enlarged** (a *maximal* one) is a
  consistent position answering every attack on its members, to which no other
  party can be added without losing that. "Some maximal defensible position
  holds it" means a reader can hold it and lose nothing by it.

### The ratings decide one thing here

Every party but one rests on something rated `disputed`. Mark 7's case rests on
the premise that no unwritten tradition can now be shown to be apostolic. Trent
rests on tradition as a source of revelation alongside Scripture, rated
`disputed` because Geiselmann grants Session IV and denies that it canonised two
coordinate sources. The reading of
Trent as commandments of men rests on Calvin's reading, which Rome denies.

The exception is Mark 7's principle. Its text is `consensus`, and its step from
the text is `wellSupported`: no one was found who grants Mark 7 and denies that
God's word judges human tradition. So an attack on it from a party at the bottom
fails, and its attack on such a party succeeds.

### Who defeats whom

- **Mark 7's principle defeats Trent read as commandments of men, and not the
  reverse.** Read that way, Trent binds a commandment of men as God's word; the
  principle denies that any may be. The reading's reply, from a claim rated
  `disputed`, fails against the principle.
- **Mark 7's case and Trent defeat each other, whichever way Trent is read.** One
  concludes that Scripture is the sole infallible rule, the other that it is
  not; and Trent read as the apostolic word also denies the premise Mark 7's case
  needs. Each side's weakest link is `disputed`, so no rating breaks the tie.
- **Mark 7's principle and Trent do not conflict**, read as Trent states it or
  as the apostolic word (`trent_grants_marks_principle`).

### What follows

**Mark 7's principle is forced** (`marks_principle_prevails`), and it is common
ground: Rome grants it. **Trent, read as commandments of men, cannot be defended**
(`trent_as_mens_commandments_indefensible`). **Between Mark 7's case for sola
scriptura and Trent, the dispute chooses neither**: each can be defended, and
neither is forced (`mark7_case_defensible`, `mark7_case_not_forced`,
`trent_defensible_against_mark7`, `trent_not_forced_against_mark7`). Mark 7 does
not decide the Reformation's question. What would decide it is argued, not
weighed: whether any unwritten tradition can be shown to be apostolic, and, even
granting that none can, whether the principle then makes Scripture the *sole*
infallible rule. Both are rated `disputed`.

#### Strength

<a id="mark7Principle_strength"></a>
**`mark7Principle_strength`**

**Mark 7's principle does not rest on anything disputed.** The text is
`consensus`, and the step from it `wellSupported`, so its weakest link is well
supported: `2` on the scale from `0`, disputed, to `3`, consensus.

```lean
theorem mark7Principle_strength : mark7Principle.strength = 2
-- axioms: propext
```

<a id="mark7Case_strength"></a>
**`mark7Case_strength`**

Mark 7's case rests on the premise that no unwritten tradition can now be
shown to be apostolic, rated `disputed`.

```lean
theorem mark7Case_strength : mark7Case.strength = 0
-- axioms: propext
```

<a id="tridentineCase_strength"></a>
**`tridentineCase_strength`**

Trent rests on tradition as a coordinate source of revelation, rated
`disputed`.

```lean
theorem tridentineCase_strength : tridentineCase.strength = 0
-- axioms: propext
```

<a id="tridentineAsMensCommandments_strength"></a>
**`tridentineAsMensCommandments_strength`**

Trent read as commandments of men rests on everything Trent does, and on
Calvin's reading, rated `disputed`.

```lean
theorem tridentineAsMensCommandments_strength :
    tridentineAsMensCommandments.strength = 0
-- axioms: propext
```

<a id="tridentineAsApostolicWord_strength"></a>
**`tridentineAsApostolicWord_strength`**

Trent read as the apostolic word rests on everything Trent does.

```lean
theorem tridentineAsApostolicWord_strength :
    tridentineAsApostolicWord.strength = 0
-- axioms: propext
```

#### The dispute

<a id="mark7PartyNode"></a>
**`mark7PartyNode`**

The package each party argues from.

```lean
def mark7PartyNode : Mark7Party → ArgumentPackage Claim :=
  fun x =>
    match x with
    | Mark7Party.principle => mark7Principle
    | Mark7Party.mark7 => mark7Case
    | Mark7Party.trent => tridentineCase
    | Mark7Party.trentAsMensCommandments =>
      tridentineAsMensCommandments
    | Mark7Party.trentAsApostolicWord =>
      tridentineAsApostolicWord
```

<a id="mark7Dispute"></a>
**`mark7Dispute`**

The dispute over Mark 7: every party's premises have a model, every party
establishes its conclusion, and every party's inferences are rated.

```lean
def mark7Dispute : Dispute Claim Mark7Party :=
  { node := mark7PartyNode,
    consistent := mark7Dispute._proof_1,
    sound := mark7Dispute._proof_2,
    rated := mark7Dispute._proof_8 }
```

<a id="mark7Dispute_defeats"></a>
**`mark7Dispute_defeats`**

**Who defeats whom**, all 25 pairs. Mark 7's principle defeats Trent read as
commandments of men, and that reading's reply fails against it. Mark 7's case
and Trent defeat each other, as Trent states it and read either way. Nothing
else.

Every cell is computed from the parties' premises by `Horn.defeats?` and checked
by the kernel — the defeats, and the absences of defeat, alike.

```lean
theorem mark7Dispute_defeats : ∀ (i j : Mark7Party), mark7Dispute.defeats i j
    ↔ (i, j) ∈ [(Mark7Party.principle, Mark7Party.trentAsMensCommandments),
    (Mark7Party.mark7, Mark7Party.trent), (Mark7Party.mark7,
    Mark7Party.trentAsMensCommandments), (Mark7Party.mark7,
    Mark7Party.trentAsApostolicWord), (Mark7Party.trent, Mark7Party.mark7),
    (Mark7Party.trentAsMensCommandments, Mark7Party.mark7),
    (Mark7Party.trentAsApostolicWord, Mark7Party.mark7)]
-- axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound
```

<a id="mark7Dispute_supports"></a>
**`mark7Dispute_supports`**

**Nothing supports anything** in the dispute over Mark 7, in all 25 pairs: no
party's conclusion entails a claim another rests on. Mark 7's principle is
*derived* inside Mark 7's case, not assumed there, so the relation between them
is not support. Every cell is computed by `supports?` and checked by the
kernel.

```lean
theorem mark7Dispute_supports : ∀ (i j : Mark7Party), ¬mark7Dispute.supports i
    j
-- axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound
```

<a id="mark7Dispute_partOf"></a>
**`mark7Dispute_partOf`**

**Whose case is part of whose**, all 25 pairs: Trent's case is part of each
reading of it, which only adds to it; and every case is part of itself. Every
cell is computed by `partOf?` and checked by the kernel.

```lean
theorem mark7Dispute_partOf : ∀ (i j : Mark7Party), mark7Dispute.partOf i j ↔
    i = j ∨ (i, j) ∈ [(Mark7Party.trent, Mark7Party.trentAsMensCommandments),
    (Mark7Party.trent, Mark7Party.trentAsApostolicWord)]
-- axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound
```

<a id="marks_principle_stands_with_trent"></a>
**`marks_principle_stands_with_trent`**

Mark 7's principle stands with Trent, as Trent states it and read as the
apostolic word: Rome's world, in which the principle holds and some unwritten
tradition is known to be apostolic.

```lean
theorem marks_principle_stands_with_trent : mark7Dispute.StandTogether
    [Mark7Party.principle, Mark7Party.trent, Mark7Party.trentAsApostolicWord]
-- axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound
```

#### What the dispute decides

<a id="marksPrincipleUnanswered"></a>
**`marksPrincipleUnanswered`**

How the dispute is settled as far as it can be, in one stage: nothing defeats
Mark 7's principle, so it comes first; and nothing joins it. Mark 7's case has
Trent, and Trent has Mark 7's case — a standoff; Trent read as the apostolic word
has Mark 7's case; and Trent read as commandments of men has the principle
itself.

**What the dispute forces is exactly *Mark 7: God's word judges human tradition*.**

- Stage 1: *Mark 7: God's word judges human tradition*.
  - *Mark 7: God's word judges human tradition* is defeated by nothing.
- Nothing else is forced:
  - *Trent (Tradition II)* defeats *Sola scriptura from Mark 7*, and nothing forced defeats *Trent (Tradition II)*.
  - *Sola scriptura from Mark 7* defeats *Trent (Tradition II)*, and nothing forced defeats *Sola scriptura from Mark 7*.
  - *Mark 7: God's word judges human tradition* [defeats](#whereTheMensCommandmentsReadingFalls) *Trent (Tradition II), read as commandments of men*, and nothing forced defeats *Mark 7: God's word judges human tradition*.
  - *Sola scriptura from Mark 7* [defeats](#whereTheApostolicWordReadingFalls) *Trent (Tradition II), read as the apostolic word handed on unwritten*, and nothing forced defeats *Sola scriptura from Mark 7*.

**What this rests on.** The reasons state 4 defeats and 7 absences of defeat, each a cell of the defeat table, [`mark7Dispute_defeats`](#mark7Dispute_defeats), computed from the two parties' premises and checked by the kernel. Whether an attack survives turns on the attacker's weakest link and on the rating of what it attacks, so a changed rating can change the verdict. The weakest links:

- *Mark 7: God's word judges human tradition*, weakest at *well supported*:
  - an inference step — [Tanner 1990](../bibliography.md#tanner-decrees-1990), §Vatican II (1965), Dei Verbum 10; [Calvin 1960](../bibliography.md#calvin-institutes-1960), §IV.x.23; [Wenham 1953](../bibliography.md#wenham-our-lords-view-1953), pp. 15–16
- *Sola scriptura from Mark 7*, weakest at *disputed*:
  - No unwritten tradition can now be shown to be apostolic, so none can bind the conscience as the word of God — [Whitaker 1849](../bibliography.md#whitaker-disputation-1849), pp. 503–511; [Whitaker 1849](../bibliography.md#whitaker-disputation-1849), p. 594; [Westminster Assembly 1647](../bibliography.md#westminster-confession-1647), §I.6
  - an inference step — [Geiselmann 1966](../bibliography.md#geiselmann-meaning-of-tradition-1966); [Tanner 1990](../bibliography.md#tanner-decrees-1990), §Vatican I (1870), Pastor Aeternus, ch. 4; [Florovsky 1972](../bibliography.md#florovsky-bible-church-tradition-1972)
- *Trent (Tradition II)*, weakest at *disputed*:
  - Tradition is a coordinate source of revelation alongside scripture — [Tanner 1990](../bibliography.md#tanner-decrees-1990), §Trent, Session IV (1546), Decree on Sacred Books and Traditions; [Mathison 2001](../bibliography.md#mathison-shape-sola-scriptura-2001); [Geiselmann 1966](../bibliography.md#geiselmann-meaning-of-tradition-1966); [Congar 1966](../bibliography.md#congar-tradition-and-traditions-1966)
- *Trent (Tradition II), read as commandments of men*, weakest at *disputed*:
  - Tradition is a coordinate source of revelation alongside scripture — [Tanner 1990](../bibliography.md#tanner-decrees-1990), §Trent, Session IV (1546), Decree on Sacred Books and Traditions; [Mathison 2001](../bibliography.md#mathison-shape-sola-scriptura-2001); [Geiselmann 1966](../bibliography.md#geiselmann-meaning-of-tradition-1966); [Congar 1966](../bibliography.md#congar-tradition-and-traditions-1966)
  - an inference step — [Calvin 1960](../bibliography.md#calvin-institutes-1960), §IV.x.23
- *Trent (Tradition II), read as the apostolic word handed on unwritten*, weakest at *disputed*:
  - Tradition is a coordinate source of revelation alongside scripture — [Tanner 1990](../bibliography.md#tanner-decrees-1990), §Trent, Session IV (1546), Decree on Sacred Books and Traditions; [Mathison 2001](../bibliography.md#mathison-shape-sola-scriptura-2001); [Geiselmann 1966](../bibliography.md#geiselmann-meaning-of-tradition-1966); [Congar 1966](../bibliography.md#congar-tradition-and-traditions-1966)

Why *Mark 7: God's word judges human tradition* defeats *Trent (Tradition II), read as commandments of men*, at the level of the claims: [`whereTheMensCommandmentsReadingFalls`](#whereTheMensCommandmentsReadingFalls).

Why *Sola scriptura from Mark 7* defeats *Trent (Tradition II), read as the apostolic word handed on unwritten*, at the level of the claims: [`whereTheApostolicWordReadingFalls`](#whereTheApostolicWordReadingFalls).

<a id="marks_principle_prevails"></a>
**`marks_principle_prevails`**

**Mark 7's principle prevails outright, and it is common ground.** The
grounded extension — what the dispute forces before any choice between rivals —
is exactly the principle: God's word judges human tradition, and no commandment
of men may be taught as God's word. Nothing defeats it: the one party that
contradicts it, Trent read as commandments of men, rests on a reading rated
`disputed`, and its reply fails against a principle whose every link is rated
`wellSupported` or better. And Trent, as it states its position, does not
contradict it at all (`trent_grants_marks_principle`).

What this does not claim: that sola scriptura is forced. Mark 7's case for it
is not (`mark7_case_not_forced`).

```lean
theorem marks_principle_prevails : Framework.grounded mark7Dispute.defeats =
    {Mark7Party.principle}
-- axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound
```

**`mensCommandmentsReadingAnswered`**

Why Trent, read as commandments of men, cannot be defended: Mark 7's
principle defeats it, and nothing defeats the principle.

***Trent (Tradition II), read as commandments of men* cannot be defended: no admissible position holds it.**

- *Mark 7: God's word judges human tradition* [defeats](#whereTheMensCommandmentsReadingFalls) *Trent (Tradition II), read as commandments of men*, and nothing defeats *Mark 7: God's word judges human tradition*.

**What this rests on.** The reasons state 1 defeat and 5 absences of defeat, each a cell of the defeat table, [`mark7Dispute_defeats`](#mark7Dispute_defeats), computed from the two parties' premises and checked by the kernel. Whether an attack survives turns on the attacker's weakest link and on the rating of what it attacks, so a changed rating can change the verdict. The weakest links:

- *Mark 7: God's word judges human tradition*, weakest at *well supported*:
  - an inference step — [Tanner 1990](../bibliography.md#tanner-decrees-1990), §Vatican II (1965), Dei Verbum 10; [Calvin 1960](../bibliography.md#calvin-institutes-1960), §IV.x.23; [Wenham 1953](../bibliography.md#wenham-our-lords-view-1953), pp. 15–16

  - an inference step — [Geiselmann 1966](../bibliography.md#geiselmann-meaning-of-tradition-1966); [Tanner 1990](../bibliography.md#tanner-decrees-1990), §Vatican I (1870), Pastor Aeternus, ch. 4; [Florovsky 1972](../bibliography.md#florovsky-bible-church-tradition-1972)
- *Trent (Tradition II)*, weakest at *disputed*:
  - Tradition is a coordinate source of revelation alongside scripture — [Tanner 1990](../bibliography.md#tanner-decrees-1990), §Trent, Session IV (1546), Decree on Sacred Books and Traditions; [Mathison 2001](../bibliography.md#mathison-shape-sola-scriptura-2001); [Geiselmann 1966](../bibliography.md#geiselmann-meaning-of-tradition-1966); [Congar 1966](../bibliography.md#congar-tradition-and-traditions-1966)
- *Trent (Tradition II), read as the apostolic word handed on unwritten*, weakest at *disputed*:
  - Tradition is a coordinate source of revelation alongside scripture — [Tanner 1990](../bibliography.md#tanner-decrees-1990), §Trent, Session IV (1546), Decree on Sacred Books and Traditions; [Mathison 2001](../bibliography.md#mathison-shape-sola-scriptura-2001); [Geiselmann 1966](../bibliography.md#geiselmann-meaning-of-tradition-1966); [Congar 1966](../bibliography.md#congar-tradition-and-traditions-1966)

Why *Mark 7: God's word judges human tradition* defeats *Trent (Tradition II), read as commandments of men*, at the level of the claims: [`whereTheMensCommandmentsReadingFalls`](#whereTheMensCommandmentsReadingFalls).

<a id="trent_as_mens_commandments_indefensible"></a>
**`trent_as_mens_commandments_indefensible`**

**Trent, read as commandments of men, cannot be defended.** No consistent
position that answers its attackers can hold it: Mark 7's principle defeats it,
and nothing answers the principle. This is the first horn of
`whatTrentsTraditionIs`, weighed: if what Trent receives alongside Scripture
were a commandment of men, Jesus' words in Mark 7
would condemn it, at a step rated `wellSupported`.

What this does not claim: that Trent's tradition *is* a commandment of men.
Trent says the opposite, and Calvin's reading of it is rated `disputed`.

```lean
theorem trent_as_mens_commandments_indefensible : ∀ (S : Set Mark7Party),
    Framework.Admissible mark7Dispute.defeats S →
    Mark7Party.trentAsMensCommandments ∉ S
-- axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound
```

<a id="mark7StandsWithItsPrinciple"></a>
**`mark7StandsWithItsPrinciple`**

Why Mark 7's case can be defended: it stands with Mark 7's principle, and
answers every party that defeats it — Trent, read or unread — itself.

***Sola scriptura from Mark 7* is accepted on some resolution.**

- A position holding *Mark 7: God's word judges human tradition*, *Sola scriptura from Mark 7* can be held.
- None of *Mark 7: God's word judges human tradition*, *Sola scriptura from Mark 7* defeats another, and each attack on them is answered from among them:

  - *Trent (Tradition II), read as the apostolic word handed on unwritten* defeats *Sola scriptura from Mark 7*, and *Sola scriptura from Mark 7* [defeats](#whereTheApostolicWordReadingFalls) *Trent (Tradition II), read as the apostolic word handed on unwritten*.

**What this rests on.** The reasons state 6 defeats and 7 absences of defeat, each a cell of the defeat table, [`mark7Dispute_defeats`](#mark7Dispute_defeats), computed from the two parties' premises and checked by the kernel. Why *Mark 7: God's word judges human tradition* defeats *Trent (Tradition II), read as commandments of men*, at the level of the claims: [`whereTheMensCommandmentsReadingFalls`](#whereTheMensCommandmentsReadingFalls).

Why *Sola scriptura from Mark 7* defeats *Trent (Tradition II), read as the apostolic word handed on unwritten*, at the level of the claims: [`whereTheApostolicWordReadingFalls`](#whereTheApostolicWordReadingFalls).

<a id="mark7_case_defensible"></a>
**`mark7_case_defensible`**

**Sola scriptura from Mark 7 can be defended.** Some maximal defensible
position holds it, with Mark 7's principle. Every party that defeats it — Trent,
as it states its position and read either way — it defeats back.

```lean
theorem mark7_case_defensible : Framework.CredulouslyAccepted
    mark7Dispute.defeats Mark7Party.mark7
-- axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound
```

<a id="mark7AnsweredByTrent"></a>
**`mark7AnsweredByTrent`**

Why Mark 7's case is not forced: a defensible position holds Trent, and Trent
defeats it.

***Sola scriptura from Mark 7* is not accepted on every resolution.**

- A position holding *Mark 7: God's word judges human tradition*, *Trent (Tradition II)*, *Trent (Tradition II), read as the apostolic word handed on unwritten* can be held, and it holds *Trent (Tradition II)*; *Trent (Tradition II)* conflicts with *Sola scriptura from Mark 7*: *Trent (Tradition II)* defeats *Sola scriptura from Mark 7*, and *Sola scriptura from Mark 7* defeats *Trent (Tradition II)*.
- None of *Mark 7: God's word judges human tradition*, *Trent (Tradition II)*, *Trent (Tradition II), read as the apostolic word handed on unwritten* defeats another, and each attack on them is answered from among them:
  - *Sola scriptura from Mark 7* defeats *Trent (Tradition II)*, and *Trent (Tradition II)* defeats *Sola scriptura from Mark 7*.
  - *Sola scriptura from Mark 7* [defeats](#whereTheApostolicWordReadingFalls) *Trent (Tradition II), read as the apostolic word handed on unwritten*, and *Trent (Tradition II)* defeats *Sola scriptura from Mark 7*.

**What this rests on.** The reasons state 3 defeats and 13 absences of defeat, each a cell of the defeat table, [`mark7Dispute_defeats`](#mark7Dispute_defeats), computed from the two parties' premises and checked by the kernel. Whether an attack survives turns on the attacker's weakest link and on the rating of what it attacks, so a changed rating can change the verdict. The weakest links:

- *Trent (Tradition II)*, weakest at *disputed*:
  - Tradition is a coordinate source of revelation alongside scripture — [Tanner 1990](../bibliography.md#tanner-decrees-1990), §Trent, Session IV (1546), Decree on Sacred Books and Traditions; [Mathison 2001](../bibliography.md#mathison-shape-sola-scriptura-2001); [Geiselmann 1966](../bibliography.md#geiselmann-meaning-of-tradition-1966); [Congar 1966](../bibliography.md#congar-tradition-and-traditions-1966)

theorem trent_not_forced_against_mark7 : ¬Framework.SkepticallyAccepted

## TestimonyArguments.SolaScriptura.Hearings — Mark 7, heard against each reading of Trent

The dispute over Mark 7 hears Trent three ways at once: as Trent states its
position, and with its tradition read each of the two ways the dilemma
`whatTrentsTraditionIs` names. A reader usually has one reading in mind, and
asks what Mark 7 settles *if that is what Trent means*. Each question is
answered by hearing the same dispute with the other readings set aside. Nothing
is re-argued: a hearing keeps every defeat the full dispute proved.

**If Rome's tradition were the commandments of men, would Mark 7 settle
sola scriptura?** Heard against that reading alone (`mensCommandmentsHearing`),
Mark 7's case is forced — but only because nothing left in the hearing contests
it. The reading is the only party that attacks it, and the principle defeats the
reading. Mark 7's case still rests on two things rated `disputed`: that no
unwritten tradition can be shown to be apostolic, and the step from the
principle to the *sole* rule. The reading of Trent as commandments of men contests neither,
and the parties that would are set aside. This is the Protestant polemic at full
strength — and it holds only on a reading of Trent that Trent itself denies.

**If Rome's tradition is the apostolic word handed on unwritten, what does
Mark 7 settle?** Heard against that reading (`apostolicWordHearing`), only the
principle — which the reading grants. Mark 7's case and the reading defeat each
other at one premise, that no unwritten tradition can be shown to be apostolic, and
each side's weakest link is `disputed`. So the dispute chooses neither.

The difference between the two hearings is the whole of what Mark 7 contributes:
against Rome's tradition read as human, it leaves Mark 7's case unopposed;
against it read as apostolic, it leaves the question where it was. Which it is,
Mark 7 does not say.

#### Heard against the reading as commandments of men

<a id="mensCommandmentsHearing"></a>
**`mensCommandmentsHearing`**

Mark 7's principle and case, heard against Trent read as commandments of
men. Not heard: Trent as it states its position, and Trent read as the
apostolic word.

```lean
def mensCommandmentsHearing : Dispute Claim { i // i ∈ [Mark7Party.principle,
    Mark7Party.mark7, Mark7Party.trentAsMensCommandments] } :=
  mark7Dispute.restrict fun x =>
    x ∈
      [Mark7Party.principle, Mark7Party.mark7,
        Mark7Party.trentAsMensCommandments]
```

<a id="mensCommandmentsHearingSettles"></a>
**`mensCommandmentsHearingSettles`**

How the hearing is settled, in two stages: nothing defeats Mark 7's
principle, so it comes first; the principle defeats the reading, and with the
reading answered Mark 7's case has no attacker left, so it comes second.

**What the dispute forces is exactly *Mark 7: God's word judges human tradition*, *Sola scriptura from Mark 7*.**

- Stage 1: *Mark 7: God's word judges human tradition*.
  - *Mark 7: God's word judges human tradition* is defeated by nothing.
- Stage 2: *Sola scriptura from Mark 7*.
  - *Trent (Tradition II), read as commandments of men* defeats *Sola scriptura from Mark 7*, and *Mark 7: God's word judges human tradition* [defeats](#whereTheMensCommandmentsReadingFalls) *Trent (Tradition II), read as commandments of men*.
- Nothing else is forced:
  - *Mark 7: God's word judges human tradition* [defeats](#whereTheMensCommandmentsReadingFalls) *Trent (Tradition II), read as commandments of men*, and nothing forced defeats *Mark 7: God's word judges human tradition*.

**What this rests on.** The reasons state 2 defeats and 5 absences of defeat, each a cell of the defeat table, [`mark7Dispute_defeats`](#mark7Dispute_defeats), computed from the two parties' premises and checked by the kernel. Whether an attack survives turns on the attacker's weakest link and on the rating of what it attacks, so a changed rating can change the verdict. The weakest links:

- *Mark 7: God's word judges human tradition*, weakest at *well supported*:
  - an inference step — [Tanner 1990](../bibliography.md#tanner-decrees-1990), §Vatican II (1965), Dei Verbum 10; [Calvin 1960](../bibliography.md#calvin-institutes-1960), §IV.x.23; [Wenham 1953](../bibliography.md#wenham-our-lords-view-1953), pp. 15–16
- *Sola scriptura from Mark 7*, weakest at *disputed*:
  - No unwritten tradition can now be shown to be apostolic, so none can bind the conscience as the word of God — [Whitaker 1849](../bibliography.md#whitaker-disputation-1849), pp. 503–511; [Whitaker 1849](../bibliography.md#whitaker-disputation-1849), p. 594; [Westminster Assembly 1647](../bibliography.md#westminster-confession-1647), §I.6
  - an inference step — [Geiselmann 1966](../bibliography.md#geiselmann-meaning-of-tradition-1966); [Tanner 1990](../bibliography.md#tanner-decrees-1990), §Vatican I (1870), Pastor Aeternus, ch. 4; [Florovsky 1972](../bibliography.md#florovsky-bible-church-tradition-1972)
- *Trent (Tradition II), read as commandments of men*, weakest at *disputed*:
  - Tradition is a coordinate source of revelation alongside scripture — [Tanner 1990](../bibliography.md#tanner-decrees-1990), §Trent, Session IV (1546), Decree on Sacred Books and Traditions; [Mathison 2001](../bibliography.md#mathison-shape-sola-scriptura-2001); [Geiselmann 1966](../bibliography.md#geiselmann-meaning-of-tradition-1966); [Congar 1966](../bibliography.md#congar-tradition-and-traditions-1966)
  - an inference step — [Calvin 1960](../bibliography.md#calvin-institutes-1960), §IV.x.23

Why *Mark 7: God's word judges human tradition* defeats *Trent (Tradition II), read as commandments of men*, at the level of the claims: [`whereTheMensCommandmentsReadingFalls`](#whereTheMensCommandmentsReadingFalls).

<a id="mark7_forced_against_mens_commandments"></a>
**`mark7_forced_against_mens_commandments`**

**Against Rome's tradition read as commandments of men, Mark 7's case is
unopposed.** Heard against that reading alone, Mark 7's principle and Mark 7's
case for sola scriptura are both forced: the reading is the only party in the
hearing that attacks the case, and the principle defeats it.

What this does not claim: that Rome's tradition is the commandments of men —
Trent says what it receives came from Christ and the apostles, and the reading
that says otherwise is rated `disputed`. Nor that Mark 7's case is sound. It
still rests on the premise that no unwritten tradition can be shown to be apostolic,
and on a step Geiselmann and Florovsky deny, both `disputed`; no party heard
here contests either. Trent as it states its position, and Trent read as the
apostolic word, are set aside.

```lean
theorem mark7_forced_against_mens_commandments : Framework.grounded
    mensCommandmentsHearing.defeats = Solver.toSet (Witness.listSub
    (Membership.mem [Mark7Party.principle, Mark7Party.mark7,
    Mark7Party.trentAsMensCommandments]) [Mark7Party.principle,
    Mark7Party.mark7])
-- axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound
```

- *Sola scriptura from Mark 7*, weakest at *disputed*:
  - No unwritten tradition can now be shown to be apostolic, so none can bind the conscience as the word of God — [Whitaker 1849](../bibliography.md#whitaker-disputation-1849), pp. 503–511; [Whitaker 1849](../bibliography.md#whitaker-disputation-1849), p. 594; [Westminster Assembly 1647](../bibliography.md#westminster-confession-1647), §I.6
  - an inference step — [Geiselmann 1966](../bibliography.md#geiselmann-meaning-of-tradition-1966); [Tanner 1990](../bibliography.md#tanner-decrees-1990), §Vatican I (1870), Pastor Aeternus, ch. 4; [Florovsky 1972](../bibliography.md#florovsky-bible-church-tradition-1972)
- *Mark 7: God's word judges human tradition*, weakest at *well supported*:
  - an inference step — [Tanner 1990](../bibliography.md#tanner-decrees-1990), §Vatican II (1965), Dei Verbum 10; [Calvin 1960](../bibliography.md#calvin-institutes-1960), §IV.x.23; [Wenham 1953](../bibliography.md#wenham-our-lords-view-1953), pp. 15–16

Why *Sola scriptura from Mark 7* defeats *Trent (Tradition II), read as the apostolic word handed on unwritten*, at the level of the claims: [`whereTheApostolicWordReadingFalls`](#whereTheApostolicWordReadingFalls).

<a id="mark7_not_forced_against_the_apostolic_word"></a>
**`mark7_not_forced_against_the_apostolic_word`**

**So, against the apostolic word, sola scriptura from Mark 7 is not
forced.** A defensible position that cannot be enlarged holds Mark 7's
principle together with Trent read as the apostolic word, and cannot hold Mark
7's case with them. What would decide is argued, not weighed: whether any
unwritten tradition can be shown to be apostolic, and whether the principle
would then make Scripture the *sole* rule. Both are rated `disputed`, and neither is
something Mark 7 speaks to.

```lean
theorem mark7_not_forced_against_the_apostolic_word :
    ¬Framework.SkepticallyAccepted apostolicWordHearing.defeats
    ⟨Mark7Party.mark7, mark7AnsweredByTheApostolicWord._proof_2⟩
-- axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound
```
